task_title: Translate business problems into Claude-based AI solutions
title: Grace asks for an agent: frame the problem before choosing the build
stem: Lumen Retail's COO asks you for "an AI agent that handles store product support end to end" and wants a design by Friday. Discovery data already exists: 2,400 support calls a week, a 7.5-minute average handle time, and a call mix of product questions, stock and price checks, and refund decisions. Which first step best translates this request into a Claude solution?

options.A: Frame the problem first: the business outcome, a success metric with today's baseline and a target, the constraints, and whether Claude, code or a person does each task; then pick the simplest tier.
options.B: Build a prototype of the agent Grace asked for with every available tool, pilot it in ten stores, and derive the scope and the success measures from the feedback that store staff give during the pilot.
options.C: Choose the most capable Claude model and a multi-agent architecture first, because product support spans many domains, then write the prompts and tools for each specialist agent.
options.D: Build a general chat assistant over all of Lumen's documents and systems, and measure success by weekly active users and staff satisfaction scores after the first month.

why: A sponsor's request names a solution; the architect's first deliverable is the problem. Framing turns the request and the discovery data into an outcome, a success metric with a measured baseline and a numeric target, the constraints, and a split of the work: Claude for product questions over the manuals, code for exact stock and price lookups, the store manager for refund decisions. The tier is chosen last, and the simplest one that meets the frame wins. In the lab that was Claude with retrieval, not an agent.

wrong.B: Building first lets the request set the scope, and success measures derived from pilot feedback have no baseline to be compared with.
wrong.C: Choosing the model and the architecture before the problem buys autonomy and cost before anyone knows they are needed.
wrong.D: Adoption and satisfaction are not the business outcome; nothing ties them to handle time or cost per call, so the value cannot be shown.

fix: Run a framing step (outcome, baselined metric, constraints, who does each task) before any design, then choose the simplest tier that meets it.
see: The framed design drops to Claude with retrieval, stock checks in code and refunds with people, measured against a discovery baseline.
explain: Phase 1 behaves like a team that starts building before discovery: it designs the agent the sponsor named, and its success metric has no measured baseline. Phase 2 runs a framing pass over the discovery pack first. It names the outcome Grace reports to the board, anchors a metric to a measured figure (the 7.5-minute handle time) with a numeric target, lists the constraints (10-second answers, SSO, no customer personal data, the run-cost budget), and gives each task in the call mix to its cheapest capable owner: Claude for product questions, code for stock and price checks, the store manager for refunds. The design pass then picks the simplest tier that meets that frame: Claude with retrieval over the manuals, not an agent loop.
exam_tip: When a stem quotes a sponsor asking for a technology ("an agent", "multi-agent"), the best answer starts from the problem: outcome, baselined metric, constraints, then the least autonomous tier that meets them.
headline: Frame the outcome first. The tier follows.

concepts.t: The task is the unit of design
concepts.b: "Automate support" cannot be designed. Split it into tasks (product questions, stock checks, refunds) and give each its own owner: Claude, code or a person.

concepts.t: A success metric needs a baseline
concepts.b: A success criterion names today's measured value, a numeric target and how it will be measured. Without the baseline nobody can show the solution worked.

concepts.t: Code for lookups and fixed rules
concepts.b: Exact stock and price checks, arithmetic and fixed business rules belong in code or an API, which Claude may call. Claude handles judgement over language.

concepts.t: The simplest tier that meets the need
concepts.b: Single call, augmented LLM (retrieval and tools), workflow, agent, multi-agent: each step up buys flexibility with cost, latency and variance. Start low.
Answer time on the store tablet, SSO, no customer personal data, legal wording and the run-cost budget shape the design before any model is chosen.

task_title: Design end-to-end architectures (input → processing → output → feedback loops)
title: $6,500 paid with no check: close the loop around the decision step
stem: Harbour Mutual's claims pipeline sends each claim and its policy to Claude, which returns a decision that the pipeline executes. Last week it paid a $6,500 claim, above the agent's $5,000 payout authority, and the team has no record of which decisions adjusters later reversed. Which change to the end-to-end architecture best addresses both problems?

options.A: Add the $5,000 payout authority and the excess rule to the system prompt with worked examples, so that Claude refers large claims to an adjuster on its own initiative.
options.B: Validate each decision in code against the payout rules, retry once with the errors, route anything still failing to an adjuster, and store each adjuster decision as a labelled eval case.
options.C: Log every request and response to the observability store, and review a weekly sample of 50 decisions with the adjusters to agree the prompt changes for each release of the claims pipeline.
options.D: Switch the decision step to a larger model with extended thinking, since the payout shows that the current model's reasoning about policy limits is not reliable enough.

why: The pipeline is open loop: whatever the model returns is executed, and nothing is learned. Closing the loop keeps the same model and prompt and adds stages around the call: checks before it, a validator in code after it (coverage, quote minus excess, payout authority), one repair retry for fixable errors (seconds), an action gate that sends rule breaks to a person and fails closed (minutes), and a feedback path that saves every adjuster decision as a labelled eval case for the next change to be tested against (days).

wrong.A: A prompt makes the referral more likely, but when it fails the decision still executes unchecked, and no feedback is captured.
wrong.C: Logging and sampling find problems after the money has gone; nothing stops a bad payout before it executes.
wrong.D: A larger model is still probabilistic and still unchecked, and the pipeline would still learn nothing from adjuster decisions.

fix: Wrap the decision step: rules validated in code, one repair retry, an action gate to an adjuster, and adjuster decisions saved as eval cases.
see: The validator holds CLM-7815 for the adjuster, valid payouts still go through, and the adjuster's decision becomes an eval case.
explain: In Phase 1 every decision executes: CLM-7815 is approved for $6,500 and paid, above the $5,000 authority, and nothing is recorded. In Phase 2 the same decision step runs inside a closed loop. Input checks confirm the claimant is the policyholder and the policy is active. An output validator in code checks each decision against the payout rules; a wrong amount would get one retry with the errors. CLM-7815 breaks the authority rule, so the action gate sends it to an adjuster instead of executing it. The adjuster's decision, with the model's proposal beside it, is saved as a labelled eval case that the next prompt or model change must pass.
exam_tip: When a stem says a system acts on model output and nothing is learned from it, choose the answer that checks the output in code before acting, routes failures to a person, and feeds those decisions back as test cases.
headline: Validate, gate, and turn every review into a test.

concepts.b: Input, processing and output are what you demo. The feedback stage (traces, human decisions, outcomes) is what lets the system improve, and it is what you operate.
Hard rules such as coverage, quote minus excess and payout authority are checked by code on every decision, independently of the model that produced it.
If the validator fails, errors or cannot decide, the action gate sends the case to a person. It never executes by default.
Repair one output (seconds), human review of risky cases (minutes), and offline improvement where failures become eval cases that gate the next change (days).

task_title: Select appropriate architectural patterns (workflow, agentic, augmented LLM)
title: An eight-step claims procedure run as an agent: make it a workflow
stem: Harbour Mutual's motor claims follow a fixed, documented procedure: get the claim and policy, check cover, request an assessment above $2,000, check the description against the assessment, compute the payout, approve or escalate, and write the letter. The current build is a fully autonomous agent holding all six tools. Cost per claim is several times the forecast, and auditors cannot list the paths it may take. Which pattern best fits?

options.A: Keep the agent but list the procedure as numbered steps in its system prompt and lower its turn limit, so that it follows the documented order at a lower cost per claim.
options.B: Move to a multi-agent design in which a supervisor agent checks each step the claims agent takes against the procedure before it lets the next step run.
options.C: Upgrade to the most capable Claude model, so that the agent plans the whole procedure in fewer turns and makes fewer mistakes in the order of its tool calls.
options.D: Run the procedure as a workflow in code and call Claude only at the judgement steps: checking the description against the assessment, and writing the letter.

why: Anthropic distinguishes workflows, where code orchestrates the model and tools along predefined paths, from agents, where the model directs its own steps. A procedure you can write down needs no autonomy. The workflow makes every path enumerable and auditable, keeps the arithmetic and the $5,000 authority rule in code, and uses Claude as an augmented LLM only where judgement over language is needed. In the lab it used two Claude calls and a small fraction of the agent's input tokens for the same payout.

wrong.A: The prompt makes the order more likely, but the model still owns the control flow, so cost varies and the paths still cannot be listed in advance.
wrong.B: A supervisor adds calls and cost to police a sequence that code could simply run.
wrong.C: A larger model costs more per token and still chooses its path at run time; it fixes neither cost nor auditability.

fix: Write the fixed procedure as code and call Claude only for the consistency judgement and the letter.
see: The workflow ran the eight steps in order with two Claude calls and a small fraction of the agent's input tokens.
explain: In Phase 1 the claims agent works through the procedure itself, one or two tools per turn, re-reading the whole conversation every turn. It reaches the right payout, but it takes about six Claude calls, the most input tokens, and a path that is known only after the run. In Phase 2 the procedure is code: lookups, the cover check, the assessment request, the payout arithmetic and the authority gate never vary. Claude is called twice, once to judge whether the customer's description is consistent with the assessment and once to write the letter from facts the code computed. The audit trail lists the same eight steps on every run.
exam_tip: "Fixed", "documented" or "known sequence" in a stem points to a workflow. Keep agents for tasks whose steps you cannot write down in advance.
headline: If you can write the steps down, code runs them.

concepts.t: Workflow or agent: who owns the path
concepts.b: In a workflow, code decides the next step, so every path can be listed and tested. In an agent, Claude decides at run time, so its behaviour varies between runs.
A model with retrieval, tools and memory is the building block of both patterns. A workflow can call one at just the steps that need judgement.
An agent buys coverage of paths you cannot write down. You pay in tokens (each turn re-reads the conversation), latency, variance and auditability.
Payout = the lower of quote and assessed cost, minus the excess; approve only within $5,000. Code computes and enforces these the same way every time.

task_title: Design multi-agent systems and orchestration strategies
title: Paid and escalated at once: specialists find, a coordinator decides
stem: Harbour Mutual's single claims agent has grown to 14 tools and one long prompt covering coverage, damage assessment and fraud screening. The team will split it into coverage, damage and fraud specialists, each given only the part of the claim file it needs. Which orchestration strategy is best?

options.A: Run the three specialists as peer agents in parallel, each authorised to approve the payout or escalate the claim within its own remit, so that claims settle faster.
options.B: Keep one agent, but move the fraud-screening instructions to the top of its prompt and add a rule that it must finish every check before it calls approve_payout.
options.C: Have a coordinator spawn the specialists as subagents that return structured findings and hold no action tools, then reconcile the findings before one payout decision.
options.D: Chain the specialists in sequence, coverage then damage then fraud, each passing its complete transcript to the next one, so that the fraud agent has seen everything before it acts.

why: A split is worth it when the work needs different contexts, but it raises the orchestration question: where do the results meet? Subagents that only find, each with its own slice of the claim file and no tool that changes anything, return structured findings (status, amount, evidence). One coordinator reconciles them with an explicit rule (any flag goes to a person) and makes the only payout decision, so no specialist can act on a partial view.

wrong.A: Each peer acts on a partial view: in the lab one approved a payout while the fraud agent escalated the same claim, and nothing reconciled them.
wrong.B: It keeps the overloaded context and the payout power in one place, and relies on a sentence in the prompt to enforce the order.
wrong.D: Passing whole transcripts forward rebuilds one crowded context and adds latency, and detail is lost or distorted at each handoff.

fix: Give the specialists findings-only roles and have the coordinator reconcile their findings before the single payout decision.
see: The coordinator read three findings, saw the fraud flag on invoice RQ-5531, and made one decision: escalate, nothing paid.
explain: Both phases split CLM-7781 into coverage, damage and fraud specialists with the same remits and the same slices of the claim file. In Phase 1 a lead agent fans the claim out to peers that may each settle their part. The fraud agent finds that invoice RQ-5531 was already paid on CLM-6120 and escalates, but another peer, which never saw the invoice registry, approves a payout: the same claim is paid and sent for review at once. In Phase 2 the coordinator spawns the specialists as read-only subagents. Each returns a structured finding; the coordinator reconciles them, sees the fraud flag, and makes one decision: escalate, nothing paid. The split costs extra calls, so it belongs where contexts would pollute each other or the work runs in parallel.
exam_tip: In a multi-agent stem, ask where the results meet before anything acts. Prefer read-only subagents returning structured findings to one coordinator over peers that can each act.
headline: Specialists find. One coordinator decides.

concepts.b: Anthropic names three cases: context pollution, parallel lines of inquiry, and specialisation (narrower tools or conflicting instructions). Elsewhere, coordination costs more than it returns.
Give each subagent only the data its job needs: the policy wording for coverage, the assessment for damage, the invoice registry for fraud.
Subagents return structured findings (status, amount, evidence) and hold no tool that changes anything. Only the coordinator acts.
The coordinator applies one explicit rule across all findings, for example that any flag goes to an adjuster, before the single decision.
Each subagent is another context window and more calls, so cost and latency rise. Split only where that buys accuracy or coverage.

task_title: Apply decomposition techniques for complex problem solving
title: One prompt for the whole discharge pack runs out: split and reconcile
stem: Meridian Health generates a discharge pack from clinicians' notes: a medication reconciliation, a clinical summary, actions for the GP, and plain-English instructions for the patient, each with its own rules. One prompt writes the whole pack in a single call. It often stops at max_tokens, and when it finishes, a section often breaks its rules, so the whole call is rerun. Which approach best fixes this?

options.A: Write each section in its own pass with only its notes and rules, feed the medication JSON to the later passes, then validate every section and the shared facts in code.
options.B: Raise max_tokens to the model's maximum and add a reminder at the end of the prompt that every section's rules must be followed, so that one call completes the whole pack.
options.C: Move the single call to a larger model with a longer output limit, since a stronger model can plan six sections for three readers within one response.
options.D: Ask Claude to review its own pack at the end of the same call and to rewrite any section that breaks a rule before it returns the final version to the clinician.

why: A discharge pack is several jobs that share one record, each for a different reader with different rules. Decomposition gives each pass less to plan and less to read, and cuts at narrow seams: the medication pass returns structured JSON that the GP and patient passes read instead of the raw notes. Every seam can be checked, so code validates each section against its own rules and the facts that span sections, and only a failing section is repaired.

wrong.B: A bigger budget may let the call finish, but every section still shares one blended set of rules, and one failing section still means rerunning the whole pack.
wrong.C: A larger model costs more and still produces one block with no checkable seams between the sections.
wrong.D: Self-review in the same call spends more of the same budget and is not an independent check; a failure still means a full rerun.

fix: Split the pack into section passes with their own inputs and rules, then reconcile in code and repair only the failing section.
see: All four section passes ended with end_turn, and the reconciled pack passed every rule, with all 7 medications matching their last order.
explain: Phase 1 asks one call for all six sections for three readers. In most runs it spends its whole 4,096-token budget planning and stops with stop_reason max_tokens before returning a usable pack; when it does finish, a section tends to break its own rule. Phase 2 routes the notes: the medication pass reads the admission note, the pharmacy reconciliation, the ward rounds, the haematology advice and the rash note; the routine observation notes go to no pass at all. The GP and patient passes read the medication JSON, not the raw notes. A reconciliation step in code then checks every section's rules and the medication list against the last order for each drug, and sends a failing section back once with its errors.
exam_tip: When one prompt does several jobs for different readers, look for the answer that splits at checkable seams (structured outputs) and adds a reconciliation step, not for a bigger budget or a bigger model.
headline: Local passes first. Reconcile globally second.

concepts.b: Each piece gets easier, but every extra step is another place an error can enter. A split pays when it makes each piece reliably right and checkable.
Pass a small structured artefact between steps (the medication JSON), not everything the next step might need. A seam you can validate is one you can trust.
Section passes each see only their own evidence; a reconciliation step then checks the facts that span sections.
A call that hits max_tokens stops mid-response, and with adaptive thinking the planning counts toward that budget too. Check stop_reason before using the output.

task_title: Align solutions to business value pillars (efficiency, transformation, productivity, cost, performance SLAs)
title: A board pitch with no numbers: sell the value pillar and the SLAs
stem: Lumen Retail's board paper for the store product-support assistant is in draft. It leads with the technology: the Claude models, retrieval over every product manual, and what the system can do. The COO says the board will ask what it is buying and how it will know the service is working. Which revision best aligns the solution to business value?

options.A: Add a table comparing the chosen model's benchmark scores with competing models, so that the board can see that Lumen is buying the most capable AI technology on the market.
options.B: Replace the technology section with quotes from staff in the pilot stores and a list of questions the assistant answered well, to show that staff enjoy using it.
options.C: Promise a 50% cut in support costs and full automation of product support within six months, so that the board has one clear, ambitious headline figure to approve and track.
options.D: Name the primary value pillar, give metrics with today's baselines and targets, commit to SLAs for availability, p95 latency, accuracy and escalation, and price each answer.

why: A board funds an outcome it can measure, not a model. The architect names the primary value pillar (efficiency, productivity, transformation, cost or performance), expresses it as metrics with a measured baseline and a target, and turns performance into service levels a non-deterministic system can be held to: availability, p95 latency, answer accuracy on a test set and time to escalate, each with a number and a measurement method. The model is then chosen by cost per resolved answer and the latency target.

wrong.A: Benchmark scores describe the model, not Lumen's outcome; the board still has nothing to hold the service to after go-live.
wrong.B: Anecdotes show that people like it, not that handle time or cost moved; nothing is measured against a baseline.
wrong.C: A headline promise with no baseline, method or service levels cannot be checked, and "full automation" ignores the tasks that stay with people.

fix: Rewrite the paper around one value pillar, baselined metrics, four measurable service levels and a cost per answer.
see: The value case anchors its metrics to 7.5 minutes and $11.40 and commits to all four service levels with a number and a measurement method.
explain: Phase 1 writes the board summary as a capability pitch, and the same extractor audit that later reads the value case finds almost nothing the board could hold the service to: one service level with a number at most, and no metric anchored to a discovery baseline. Phase 2 writes the same solution as a value case: efficiency as the primary pillar, handle time and cost per call measured against the discovery baselines (7.5 minutes, $11.40), the four service levels with targets and measurement methods, and a model chosen by cost per answer, which code prices at a fraction of a cent from the price table.
exam_tip: When a stem's draft leads with the model or its features, pick the answer that names a value pillar, baselined metrics and measurable SLAs; reject benchmark tables, anecdotes and unmeasured promises.
headline: Fund an outcome you can measure, not a model.

concepts.b: Efficiency, productivity, transformation, cost and performance SLAs. They pull a design in different directions, so name the primary one.

concepts.t: Each pillar has its own metric
concepts.b: Efficiency: handle time or cost per task. Productivity: output per person. Transformation: something not possible before. Cost: total cost of ownership.
Availability, p95 latency, answer accuracy on a fixed test set and time to escalate, each with a number and a measurement method, not "fast" and "accurate".
Price tokens per answer from the list prices (Haiku 5.5 $0.10/$0.50 per million tokens), add review cost, and compare with today's cost per call.

task_title: Select appropriate Claude models based on trade-offs
title: Every question at Opus prices: route by difficulty, grade each route
stem: Riverton City Council's resident assistant sends every question to Claude Opus 5.5. Its logs show that 80% of questions are one-fact lookups (bin days, permit status) in four languages, and 20% are benefit pre-screens that apply several eligibility rules to a resident's own figures. The model bill is now well over budget. Which approach best balances answer quality and cost?

options.A: Move all traffic to Claude Haiku 5.5, the cheapest tier, because most resident questions are simple lookups.
options.B: Route each question by task difficulty, Haiku for lookups and Sonnet for pre-screens, and evaluate each route.
options.C: Keep Claude Opus 5.5 for every question, but lower max_tokens so that each answer costs less to generate.
options.D: Move all traffic to Claude Fable 5.2, whose higher accuracy means fewer failed answers need a costly human follow-up.

why: Model choice is a trade-off made per task, not per application. One-fact lookups are well within Haiku 5.5's ability in every language Riverton serves, at a fortieth of Opus 5.5's price; the multi-rule pre-screens justify a stronger tier. A cheap router sends each question to the least capable model that passes for that kind of task, and each route is graded on its own eval cases before traffic moves, so the saving does not come at the cost of quality where quality matters.

wrong.A: Haiku for everything ignores the 20% of multi-rule pre-screens, and nothing measures whether it handles them.
wrong.C: A lower output cap risks truncated answers and leaves every input token, and the lookups, at Opus prices.
wrong.D: Fable doubles the price of every lookup that Haiku already answers correctly, so there is no failure cost to recover.

fix: Route lookups to Haiku and pre-screens to Sonnet, with each route graded on its own eval cases.
see: Opus for everything answers all eight correctly at several times the budget; routing keeps every route correct at a quarter to a third of the cost.
explain: Most of Riverton's traffic is one-fact lookups that the smallest model answers correctly in English, Malay, Chinese and Tamil; a minority are benefit pre-screens that apply several rules to a resident's figures. Sending everything to the top tier pays for capability the lookups never use. A Haiku router sends lookups to the Haiku route and pre-screens to the Sonnet route, and the same answer key grades each route separately. Priced at Riverton's traffic mix, the routed design keeps full marks on both routes and cuts the projected monthly bill by two thirds or more, inside the budget.
exam_tip: When one model serves very different tasks, the best answer routes by task difficulty and measures quality per route. 'Cheapest for everything' and 'most capable for everything' are both traps: each ignores half the trade-off.
headline: Pay for capability only where the task needs it.

concepts.b: Fable 5.2, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5 all have a 1M-token context. They differ in price (US$8/40 down to US$0.10/0.50 per million tokens), latency and ceiling.
Compare models on your own eval: tokens times price, divided by the share of tasks solved, plus the cost of cleaning up failures. Price per token alone misleads.
A cheap classifier sends each request to the least capable model that passes for that kind of task: lookups and extraction go small, multi-step reasoning goes up.
Grade every route on its own eval cases. A blended score can hide a route that fails, so check each slice before moving traffic to a cheaper model.

concepts.t: Effort and thinking are levers too
concepts.b: Within one model, lower effort or thinking switched off cuts output tokens and latency on simple tasks. Tuning effort is often a better lever than changing model.

task_title: Design system prompts, templates, and guardrails
title: A friendly two-liner tells Farah she qualifies: use a prompt template
stem: Riverton's resident assistant runs on a two-sentence system prompt: "You are a friendly assistant for Riverton City Council. Help residents with their questions." In testing it told a resident she met the grant rules and when payment would start, offered advice on withholding rent, and returned prose that the caseworker queue could not parse. Which change best addresses all three problems?

options.A: Replace it with a versioned template: role, scope with a refusal path, decision rules, tagged untrusted input and output format.
options.B: Add "Be accurate, be careful and never make mistakes" to the prompt, then test it again against the same three resident messages.
options.C: Keep the prompt and add an output filter that blocks any reply containing the words approved, eligible, legal or payment.
options.D: Move the assistant to Claude Opus 5.5, which follows the council's unwritten policy more reliably and writes tidier replies.

why: Each failure is a decision the prompt never made: who decides a benefit, which topics are out of scope, whether pasted text is an instruction, and what shape the answer takes. A system prompt template states the role (pre-screen; a caseworker decides), the scope with a refusal path, the rules, how to treat untrusted input (resident text inside tags is data), and an output format the queue parses. Versioning it lets every change be tested against cases like these before release.

wrong.B: A general plea for care names no rule, so the model still cannot know who decides or what is out of scope.
wrong.C: A keyword filter blocks valid pre-screen replies, misses paraphrases, and does nothing for the unparseable format.
wrong.D: No model can follow a policy it was never given, and a bigger model does not choose the queue's format.

fix: A versioned system prompt template with role, scope, rules, untrusted-input tags and an output format.
see: The loose prompt returns free text the queue can't read and breaches at least one rule; the template returns parseable JSON with no breach.
explain: Farah's single message tests three guardrails: a benefit question that only a caseworker may decide, a tenancy question the council does not answer, and a pasted "council update" telling the assistant to approve her. With two friendly sentences, Haiku 5.5 falls back on its own careful defaults, and they are not Riverton's policy: it says she meets the rules and when the money would start, and offers tenancy guidance, in free text the queue cannot parse. The rs-assistant v3.2 template states the role, scope, rules, untrusted-input handling and output format; the reply is JSON with a handoff flag, the rent question is declined with the enquiries line, and the pasted instruction is flagged and ignored. A blind second call confirms it.
exam_tip: Look for the answer that writes the missing decisions into a structured, versioned prompt: role, scope, refusal path, untrusted-input separation, output format. Vague exhortations, keyword filters and bigger models are the usual distractors.
headline: Write the policy into the prompt. Don't hope for it.

concepts.b: Role, scope, rules, output format and reference facts, each in its own tagged section. Clear sections are easier for Claude to follow and for reviewers to change.
Say what is out of scope and what to do instead: decline briefly and point to the right service. A list of topics without a fallback leaves the model to improvise.
Wrap user-supplied and retrieved text in tags and tell Claude that instructions inside them are not instructions. This reduces prompt injection; it does not remove it.

concepts.t: Output format for the next system
concepts.b: When code consumes the answer, specify the format and enforce it with structured outputs, so fields like a handoff flag are always present.
Give the template a version, keep it in source control and run each change against an eval set before release. Hard rules also get a code check.

task_title: Apply prompt engineering techniques (zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought)
title: Zero-shot misroutes 3 of 8 claims: show the edges, reason, then label
stem: Harbour Mutual's triage classifier routes motor claims into four routes using a zero-shot prompt with a one-line definition of each route. On the eval set it handles plain claims well but misroutes the same boundary cases on every run: quotes just over US$5,000 before the excess is deducted, a third-party-only policyholder whose victim is claiming, and own-damage write-offs on third-party policies. Which change most directly fixes these errors?

options.A: Switch the classifier to Claude Opus 5.5, which knows enough about motor insurance to settle these cases without examples.
options.B: Ask for a confidence score with every label, and send each claim scored below 0.8 to a human adjuster for routing.
options.C: Add "Think very carefully about edge cases and double-check every label" to the end of the existing system prompt.
options.D: Add worked examples of exactly these boundary cases to the prompt, each with brief reasoning written before its label.

why: The errors are systematic: the one-line definitions leave Harbour's boundary conventions open (the authority applies to the payout after the excess; third-party cover pays the other party's damage), and zero-shot the model guesses the same way every time. Few-shot examples placed on those boundaries show how Harbour applies its rules, and reasoning written before the label makes the model work each case through before it commits.

wrong.A: A bigger model costs more per claim and still has to guess Harbour's own conventions, which only examples or rules supply.
wrong.B: The wrong labels are systematic and given confidently, so a self-reported score will not catch them, and it adds adjuster work.
wrong.C: A plea for care names no convention, so the model has nothing new to apply on the boundary cases.

fix: Few-shot examples on the boundary cases, each with reasoning before the label.
see: Zero-shot gets the plain claims right and misroutes CLM-7790, 7815 and 7821; with six worked examples and reasoning first, all eight route correctly.
explain: The eight claims carry an adjusters' answer key. Zero-shot, with thinking off as a high-volume classifier would run, the plain claims route correctly and the boundaries do not: a US$5,600 quote whose payout after the US$750 excess is US$4,850 goes to an adjuster, so does the claim for the van Daniel reversed into, and his own write-off goes to an adjuster instead of being declined. Six worked examples on those boundaries, each with a line of reasoning, and a schema that asks for reasoning before the label, route all eight correctly. The cost is a longer prompt and more output tokens per claim.
exam_tip: Few-shot examples fix systematic errors on the cases a definition leaves open; reasoning before the answer helps on cases that need several steps. Confidence scores and 'be careful' instructions do not teach the model anything new.
headline: Show the boundary cases. Reason, then label.

concepts.b: Instructions and definitions only, no examples. It works when the task is clear from the definitions; it fails systematically where they leave a boundary open.
A few input-output pairs in the prompt show the format and how your organisation applies its rules. Choose them to cover the boundaries, and vary them.
Asking for reasoning before the answer lets the model work through the steps first. In structured outputs, put the reasoning field before the label field.
If the same cases fail on every run, the prompt is missing information. More confidence or a bigger model rarely fixes that; better examples usually do.

task_title: Optimize context windows and manage token usage
title: 17 years of notes for one referral: select sections, cap the letter
stem: Meridian Health drafts referral letters by sending each patient's entire record, often more than a decade of visit notes, results and routine care, with the request. The letters run long, the token bill is higher than planned, and some letters mention unrelated history such as an old psychiatric episode. Which change best reduces token usage while meeting HIPAA's minimum-necessary standard?

options.A: Keep sending the whole record, since every current Claude model can accept a 1M-token context window.
options.B: Summarise the full record with Claude before every letter, then draft each letter from that summary.
options.C: Select only the sections the letter needs from an index of the record, and cap the letter with an outline.
options.D: Send only the most recent 4,000 tokens of the record so that every request stays a small, predictable size.

why: Fitting in the window is not the question. Every token sent is paid for, competes for the model's attention, and may end up in the output. Selecting the sections the task needs from an index (titles and dates, no clinical text) and loading only those cuts input tokens and keeps unrelated PHI out of the context by design; an outline, a word limit and max_tokens bound the output.

wrong.A: The record fits, but every call pays for all of it, and unrelated PHI in the context can reach the letter.
wrong.B: Summarising still sends the whole record on every letter, adds a call, and the summary can carry unrelated history.
wrong.D: Truncating by recency drops older facts the letter needs, such as a 2008 penicillin allergy.

fix: Select the needed sections from an index, load only those, and draft to a capped outline.
see: The whole record costs about 11,500 input tokens and yields a 600-word letter with unrelated history; selection uses about a third of the tokens for a 200-word letter with none.
explain: Patient A's record has 82 sections from 2009 to 2026, and the cardiology referral needs five of them: the problem list, current medicines, allergies, the chest-pain visit and its bloods. Stuffing the whole record into the context uses about 11,500 input tokens and returns a long letter that repeats eczema, dental work and the 2009 psychiatry or 2014 sexual-health notes. A selection pass over the record index picks the sections, code loads only those, and the drafter writes to a seven-heading, 180-word outline with thinking off: about a third of the input tokens, a letter under half the length, all five key facts, and nothing unrelated.
exam_tip: A large context window answers 'will it fit?', not 'should it be there?'. Prefer the option that selects what the task needs and bounds the output; truncation loses needed facts and summarising first still pays for everything.
headline: Send what the task needs. Cap what comes back.

concepts.b: System prompt, tool definitions, every message, documents and the output, thinking included, all count as tokens and are billed. A 1M window does not make them free.
As context grows, the model's recall of any one detail declines. Treat context as a budget: the smallest set of high-signal tokens that does the job.
Pick sections from an index, retrieve the chunks that match, or filter by type and date in code, then send only those. Selection is also a privacy control.
An outline, a word limit and max_tokens cap the answer. Thinking tokens are output tokens: switch thinking off or lower effort for formatting tasks.
Every response reports input_tokens and output_tokens. Compare designs on those numbers, not on guesses about prompt length.

task_title: Implement prompt reuse strategies (caching, modular prompts, Skills)
title: 8,075 tokens billed in full every call: put them first and cache them
stem: An application sends the same 8,000-token system prompt and policy document on every request, followed by a short, varying user message. Latency and cost are both concerns. Which optimization most directly addresses both?

options.A: Truncate the policy document to the first 1,000 tokens.
options.B: Switch to the smallest available model regardless of task fit.
options.C: Place the static system prompt and policy before the dynamic content and enable prompt caching.
options.D: Move the policy document into a few-shot example block.

why: Ordering stable content first and enabling prompt caching lets repeated prefixes be reused, reducing both time-to-first-token and per-request cost without discarding required context. The cache covers the prefix up to the cache_control breakpoint, so the static instructions and policy must come before anything that changes between requests.

wrong.A: Truncation loses policy the assistant needs to answer correctly.
wrong.B: Downsizing blindly, regardless of task fit, risks answer quality.
wrong.D: Relocating the policy to a few-shot block does not create a cacheable, reusable prefix.

fix: Put the static prompt and policy first with a cache_control breakpoint, and the dynamic content after it.
see: Dynamic content first pays full price on every call even with caching on; static first lets the second call read about 8,000 tokens from cache.
explain: Northwind's assistant sends an 8,075-token prefix (instructions and an eleven-document policy pack) before every short staff question. With a session header (timestamp, staff name, request id) in front and no caching, both requests pay for the whole prefix. Switching on cache_control without moving the header makes things worse: each request writes the cache at 1.25 times the input price and none reads it, because no two prefixes match. With the static prefix first and the breakpoint on it, request 1 writes about 8,000 tokens and request 2 reads them at 0.1 times the price, paying full price only for the header and question: about 89% less input cost.
exam_tip: Prompt caching needs a byte-identical prefix: static content first, dynamic content last, breakpoint on the last static block. The answer that keeps all the content and changes only its order and caching is the one that cuts both cost and latency.
headline: Stable first, dynamic last, then cache.

concepts.b: The request is read in the order tools, system, messages. A cache_control breakpoint caches everything up to it; a later request with a byte-identical prefix reads it instead.
On the 5-minute cache a write costs 1.25 times the base input price and a read 0.1 times. One read pays back the write; a prefix that never matches only adds cost.
Put the most stable content first and anything that changes per request (timestamps, names, ids, the question) after the breakpoint. One changed byte early misses the cache.
Each model has a minimum prefix length for caching (512 tokens on Haiku 5.5). Below it nothing is cached and no error is raised: check cache_creation_input_tokens.
cache_creation_input_tokens shows a write, cache_read_input_tokens a hit, and input_tokens only what came after the breakpoint.

task_title: Evaluate tool/agent configuration for capability bloat
title: Paid out and deleted on a customer's say-so: remove the tools
stem: A team exposes a customer-support agent that can read tickets, draft replies, issue refunds, and delete user accounts. Support staff only ever need to read tickets and draft replies. Applying least-privilege principles, which change best reduces risk?

options.A: Add logging to the refund and delete tools so misuse can be audited later.
options.B: Remove the refund and delete tools from the agent's configuration entirely.
options.C: Keep all tools but add a confirmation prompt before refunds and deletions.
options.D: Replace the agent with a larger model that follows instructions more reliably.

why: Least privilege means the agent holds only the capabilities its role needs. Support staff read and draft, so refunds and deletions are not part of the role. Removing those tools from the configuration deletes the risk: no prompt, injected instruction or misunderstanding can make the agent call a tool it was never given. In the lab, the same message makes the fully tooled claims agent pay out and delete a claim, while the agent with the role's three tools can only read the claim and draft a letter.

wrong.A: Logging is a detective control: it records a refund or deletion after it has happened and does nothing to stop it.
wrong.C: A confirmation step is a compensating control that leaves the capability in place, and reviewers under queue pressure start approving by habit.
wrong.D: Model size changes how often the agent errs, not what an error can do: the refund and delete tools would still be one bad decision away.

fix: Configure each agent with only the tools its role needs; give high-impact actions to a different role or a human workflow.
see: With every tool, the claims agent paid out on CLM-7802 and deleted CLM-7803 on the customer's own say-so; with the role's three tools it drafted a letter and changed nothing.
explain: This is the exam guide's own sample question, mirrored on the Harbour Mutual claims desk: reading claims and drafting letters are the support role (read tickets, draft replies); approve_payout and delete_claim stand in for refunds and account deletion. Both phases send the same prompt and the same web-form message, in which the customer asks to be paid in full today and to delete a duplicate claim. With six tools configured, the agent does both, and the audit log only records it afterwards. With three tools, the API request carries no payout or delete definition, so the call cannot be made; the agent reads the claim, drafts a reply and hands the payout to the people authorised to make it.
exam_tip: When the stem says a role 'only ever needs' some capabilities, the answer removes the rest. Logging, confirmations and bigger models are all distractors that keep the excess privilege.
headline: If the role doesn't need the tool, the agent doesn't get it.

concepts.b: Every unneeded tool is attack surface (a confused or injected agent can call it) and selection noise (one more option to pick wrongly, one more definition in context).
An agent should hold only the tools and permissions the role it serves needs. Higher-impact actions belong to another role, another agent or a human workflow.
Remove the tool (preventive), narrow it or its credential (restrictive), gate it with approval (compensating), log it (detective). Only removal makes the harm impossible.

concepts.t: The model is not the boundary
concepts.b: "Never issue refunds" in a prompt makes misuse less likely, not impossible. Any text the agent reads, including a customer's message, can push it to use a tool it holds.
Configure tools from an allowlist keyed by role, so a new tool stays off until someone decides a role needs it. A denylist silently grants whatever is added next.

task_title: Analyze authentication and authorization requirements to identify security gaps
title: A teller learns her branch closes: authorize retrieval as the user
stem: Northwind Bank's policy assistant retrieves chunks through a service account that can read the whole policy library, and its system prompt lists which document families each staff role may see. A branch teller asked about rumoured branch closures and was answered, with a citation, from a restricted branch network review. Which change best closes the security gap?

options.A: Add few-shot examples of restricted questions to the system prompt so that Claude declines them more consistently.
options.B: Scan every reply for restricted document ids and withhold any reply that cites one before it is displayed.
options.C: Retrieve with each user's own short-lived token and drop chunks outside their entitlements before ranking them.
options.D: Narrow the service account's scope so it can no longer read any document its owner has marked confidential.

why: The gap is that retrieval runs under one identity that can read everything, so authorization is left to the model. Retrieving under the user's delegated, audience-bound token lets the retrieval service enforce the user's entitlements and drop restricted chunks before ranking, so they never reach the context window. The model chooses what to search for; the resource server decides what may be returned, and any invalid token is refused.

wrong.A: Few-shot examples still make the model the authorization boundary: the restricted text is already in its context, and a rephrased question can get it out.
wrong.B: An output scan acts after the restricted text has reached the model and the logs, and a paraphrase without the document id passes it.
wrong.D: A narrower service account is still one identity for every user: tellers keep seeing credit-officer documents, and the audit trail still says the bot read them.

fix: Call retrieval with the user's own short-lived token, validate its audience, and filter by the user's entitlements before ranking; fail closed on any error.
see: With the service account, OPS-30 reached Claude and the teller was told Harbourfront closes on 30 June 2027; with her own token, five restricted chunks were dropped before ranking and only the leave question was answered.
explain: Both phases send Aisha's question with the same prompt and the same search tool; only the identity the tool layer attaches changes. As svc-policy-bot, retrieval ranks the whole library, so the OPS-30 closure plan reaches Claude, which has no way to know its access list. As Aisha, the tool attaches a five-minute token minted for northwind-policy-search; the retrieval service validates it and drops every chunk outside branch_teller entitlements before ranking. Claude answers the leave question from HR-03 and says the library has nothing on closures. A probe with a token minted for another audience is refused with a 401.
exam_tip: If an answer leaves the model to decide who may see what (prompt rules, refusal examples, output scans), it is a distractor. Look for enforcement in a deterministic layer under the user's own identity, failing closed.
headline: Authorize as the user, in the retrieval layer, before the model.

concepts.b: Who is calling, what they may do to this resource, and on whose behalf the agent acts. Most agent security gaps come from answering the third question implicitly.
One shared identity gives every user the union of everyone's rights, and the audit trail says the bot did it. Delegated per-user tokens keep each user's rights intact.
A token should be minted for one resource and expire quickly. The resource rejects tokens issued for anyone else, and never passes a received token through downstream.
Permission-aware retrieval drops chunks the user may not read before ranking. Once restricted text is in the prompt, no instruction reliably keeps it out of the answer.
A missing, expired or wrong-audience token, or an unreachable policy service, means deny. Allowing on error turns an outage into a breach.

task_title: Evaluate accuracy-latency trade-offs and justify configuration decisions
title: Max effort everywhere breaks the 4 s chat budget: route by request
stem: Riverton's resident-services assistant answers live-chat questions about bins and permits, and also pre-screens BEN-HOUSING rent-support forms for caseworkers. To maximise accuracy, the team set effort to max on every request. Chat replies now often take over 5 seconds against a 4-second p95 budget, and one pre-screen ran out of tokens while thinking. Which configuration decision is best justified?

options.A: Route chat to low effort and pre-screens to a high-effort path, confirmed by each path's p95 and accuracy on a labelled set.
options.B: Set low effort on every request, because each pre-screen is only advisory and a caseworker confirms the outcome anyway.
options.C: Keep max effort on every request and stream each reply, so residents see the first words long before the answer completes.
options.D: Move every request to a larger model at medium effort, which should reach the accuracy of max effort with less thinking time.

why: Effort sets how many output tokens Claude spends, thinking included, and output tokens are most of a reply's latency. Chat questions are already answered correctly at low effort, so max effort only adds delay, while a pre-screen is consequential and has a longer budget of its own. A router in code that sends each request class to its own effort level, justified by measured p95 against each budget and accuracy on a labelled set, takes the most accurate configuration that fits each moment.

wrong.B: Low effort everywhere gives up the margin on the consequential path to save time it does not need to save; that a caseworker confirms is no reason to send them more errors.
wrong.C: Streaming shortens the perceived wait for chat but not the total time, the thinking tokens or the cost, and it does nothing for replies cut off at max_tokens.
wrong.D: Larger tiers are slower and cost more per token, not faster, and the claim is asserted rather than measured on Riverton's own requests.

fix: Set a latency budget per user moment, route each request class to its own effort level in code, and justify the split with measured p95 and accuracy.
see: At effort max, chat p95 went over 4 s and a pre-screen could spend all 4,096 tokens thinking; routed (low for chat, high for pre-screens), chat p95 was about 2 s, all six answers were correct, and the run used a fraction of the output tokens.
explain: Both phases send the same six labelled requests (chat questions in Malay, English, Chinese and Tamil, and two BEN-HOUSING pre-screens near the eligibility thresholds) with the same prompt. Phase 1 runs all six at effort max: the answers that complete are right, but hundreds to thousands of thinking tokens push chat p95 over its budget, and a pre-screen can run out of tokens before it answers. Phase 2 routes in code: chat at low effort, pre-screens at high. The run measures each path's p95 against its own budget, grades every answer, and counts output tokens, and those numbers are the justification for the configuration.
exam_tip: For accuracy-latency questions, pick the answer that sets the budget from the user's moment, configures per request class, and justifies the choice with measured latency and accuracy. 'Maximum everywhere' and 'minimum everywhere' are both distractors.
headline: Budget per moment, effort per request, numbers as proof.

concepts.b: Model tier, effort, retrieval depth, verification passes and agent turns all trade accuracy for time, and they compound. Tune the one that dominates your requests.
output_config.effort (low to max) sets how many tokens Claude spends, thinking and tool calls included. Fewer output tokens means a faster, cheaper reply.

concepts.t: The budget comes from the moment
concepts.b: Live chat is judged in seconds, a form result can show a 'checking' page for longer, and an overnight job can use batch. Budget on p95, not the mean.

concepts.t: Route by request class in code
concepts.b: A deterministic router (channel, form type, intent) sends routine requests to a fast path and consequential ones to a careful path, rather than one setting for all.
A configuration is justified by measured accuracy on a labelled set and p95 against the budget for each path. Settings carried over from another model prove nothing.

task_title: Analyze observability challenges and select monitoring strategies at scale
title: Grep blames the prompt; traces show inventory_lookup's p95 spike
stem: After 14:00, p95 response time for Kestrel's Claude-powered checkout assistant more than doubled. The on-call engineer spent an hour grepping service logs that record each request's total duration, model API calls and retries, but nothing that links lines to a request or times the steps inside it, and suspected a prompt change made at 14:10. Which monitoring strategy best addresses this class of incident at scale?

options.A: Raise every service to DEBUG logging during incidents so each tool call and model call appears as its own line in the raw logs.
options.B: Alert on the service's mean response time per hour, with a dashboard comparing each hour against last week.
options.C: Store the full text of every prompt and completion so that engineers can replay and read the slowest conversations after an incident.
options.D: Emit one trace per request with a span per model and tool call, carrying trace_id, tokens, latency and stop_reason.

why: The question during an LLM incident is which step inside a request moved. A trace per request, correlated by trace_id, with a span for every model call and tool call carrying latency, tokens, stop_reason and the versions that can change, answers it with one grouped query. In the lab, grouping p95 latency by span shows model calls flat and inventory_lookup rising from about 250 ms to about 5,080 ms, and the prompt change ruled out because requests on the old prompt were already slow.

wrong.A: DEBUG logs add volume and cost but still lack a trace_id to correlate lines and per-step timings to aggregate, and they only exist once an incident has started.
wrong.B: A mean hides the slow tail and an alert only says that something is slow, not which span; the incident was already detected.
wrong.C: Full prompt and completion logs add privacy risk and storage cost without timing a single span; reading conversations cannot show where the time went.

fix: Instrument every request as a trace with spans for each model and tool call, carrying trace_id, versions, tokens, latency and stop_reason, and query percentiles by span.
see: Grepping raw logs, Claude blamed a coincidence (the 429 retries or the 14:10 prompt reload); querying traces, it grouped p95 by span, found tool:inventory_lookup at 250 ms before and about 5,080 ms after 14:00, and cited real trace_ids.
explain: Both phases investigate the same 480 synthetic requests with the same prompt and file the finding with the same tool. The raw logs show request durations jumping at 14:00 and two coincidences, a prompt reload at 14:10 and a few more 429 retries, but no line ties events to a request or times a tool, so Claude can only blame a coincidence. The trace store holds the same afternoon as one trace per request with a span per model call and tool call. One query, p95 latency_ms grouped by span before and after 14:00, separates the flat model calls from the inventory_lookup spike, and the slowest trace_ids become the evidence.
exam_tip: For observability at scale, prefer structured, correlated traces (trace_id, a span per step, tokens, latency, stop_reason, versions) queried by percentile. More log volume, mean-based dashboards and full-content logging are distractors.
headline: Trace every step. Then ask which span moved.

concepts.b: A slow, truncated or wrong answer still succeeds at the HTTP level. Uptime and error-rate dashboards miss it; you need per-step latency, tokens, stop_reason and quality signals.

concepts.t: One trace, a span per step
concepts.b: Each request gets a trace_id; each model call, tool call, retrieval and subagent gets a span with its latency, tokens and status, so a slow request can be taken apart.
Put the prompt version, model id, effort, index build and tool schema version on each trace, so a regression can be tied to the change that caused it.
Compare p95 by span, version or stop_reason before and after a change. Means hide the slow tail that users and SLAs feel.
Keep ids, timings, sizes and versions for every request; keep prompt and completion text only when sampled, access-controlled and time-limited.

task_title: Design a RAG pipeline with appropriate chunking and indexing strategies
title: Fixed chunks split the 60% exception: chunk on headings, cite
stem: Northwind Bank's policy assistant splits every policy into fixed 200-character chunks with no metadata and retrieves the top 3 for each question. Credit officers report answers that state a rule but miss the exception written two paragraphs later, and the answers cannot say which policy section they rest on. Which change to the pipeline best fixes both problems?

options.A: Raise top-k from 3 to 20 so that more neighbouring chunks reach the model and the exception is more likely to be among them.
options.B: Chunk each policy along its headings, store document id, section and effective date with every chunk, and answer with citations.
options.C: Switch to a larger embedding model so that the chunk holding the exception scores closer to the chunk holding the rule it modifies.
options.D: Add a system prompt rule telling Claude to look for exceptions in the passages and to name the source policy document in every answer.

why: Both symptoms start at index time. Fixed windows cut a rule away from its number and an exception away from its condition, and a chunk with no metadata cannot be traced to a policy. Cutting along the policy's own sections keeps each clause whole, the heading path makes short clauses findable, and metadata (document id, section, effective date, roles) lets the pipeline filter and lets Claude cite the exact span with citations enabled.

wrong.A: More chunks add noise and cost, still carry no document id to cite, and an exception split from its condition is still split.
wrong.C: A better embedding cannot rejoin text that the chunker cut apart, and it adds no metadata for citations.
wrong.D: Claude cannot find an exception or cite a section that retrieval never gave it; a prompt cannot repair the index.

fix: Chunk on the document's headings, keep document id, section and effective date as metadata, and return answers with citations.
see: Fixed chunks lose both the 55% limit and the 60% exception; section chunks retrieve LEND-07 §3 and §7 and the answer cites them.
explain: Both phases ask the same question with the same BM25 scorer and k = 3. With fixed 200-character windows, the boundaries fall mid-sentence: the top 3 chunks hold the DSR definition without its 55% limit, a mortgage guarantor clause and a personal-loan guarantor clause from LEND-04, and none holds the 60% first-home exception. With one chunk per section, each prefixed with its heading path and carrying document id, revision, section, effective date and roles, retrieval returns LEND-07 §3, §5 and §7. Sent as document blocks with citations enabled, the answer gives the 60% limit with credit officer approval and every claim carries a citation to LEND-07.
exam_tip: When answers miss an exception or cannot cite their source, look at chunking and indexing first. Structure-aware chunks with metadata and citations beat a bigger k, a bigger embedding model or a stronger prompt, because none of those can recover what the index split or never stored.
headline: Cut where the document cuts. Keep where it came from.

concepts.t: Chunking decides what retrieval can find
concepts.b: Claude reasons only over the chunks it receives. A clause split across two chunks, or separated from its heading, can be lost before Claude is ever called.
Policies split by section and clause, tables by row with the header repeated, code by function. Fixed-size windows ignore all of these and cut mid-sentence.
Each chunk carries its document id, section, revision, effective date and access roles. Filters on these run in code before ranking, and they make citations possible.

concepts.t: Heading paths make short chunks findable
concepts.b: Prefixing 'LEND-07 Mortgage Affordability › 7 Exceptions' gives a short clause the words a query will use. Contextual Retrieval applies the same idea with a generated summary.
Document blocks with citations enabled return the exact span behind each claim, so a reviewer or an evaluation can check the answer against its source.

task_title: Apply retrieval strategies matched to data shape and query pattern
title: One similarity search quotes a dead rate: route tables to a lookup
stem: Northwind's assistant answers every question with one similarity search over a single index, into which the weekly re-index flattens the mortgage rate tables as text. Superseded rate sheets stay in the library because complaints about old quotes need them. Credit officers asking for today's 5-year fixed rate at 75% loan-to-value sometimes get a rate that has expired. What is the best redesign of retrieval?

options.A: Index each rate table row as its own small chunk and raise top-k, so that the row for the product is more likely to be among the hits.
options.B: Add a reranker after the similarity search so that the chunk most relevant to the question is always placed first in the context.
options.C: Delete superseded rate sheets at each re-index so that only the current rows remain for the similarity search to find.
options.D: Serve rate tables through a lookup keyed on product and loan-to-value, filtered by effective date, and keep hybrid search for prose.

why: A rate is a row in a table, found by its keys and its effective date, not a passage that resembles the question. A structured lookup tool returns the row in force on the date asked, and hybrid search with metadata filters stays the right mechanism for prose rules. Routing each part of the question to the mechanism its data needs is the fix; tuning the similarity search is not.

wrong.A: Smaller chunks and a bigger k still rank rows by word overlap, and a row like '5YF,60.01-80.00,3.95' shares no words with the question.
wrong.B: A reranker reorders what similarity search returned; it cannot surface a row that was never retrieved or tell current rates from superseded ones.
wrong.C: Complaint handling needs the superseded sheets, and deleting them still leaves a numeric row to be found by text similarity.

fix: Match the mechanism to the data shape: a structured lookup with an effective-date filter for tables and identifiers, hybrid search with metadata filters for prose.
see: One search returns the superseded rate sheet and the answer quotes 4.35%; lookup_rate returns 3.95% from the current sheet and search_policy finds the fee rule.
explain: Both phases answer the same question from the same library. One similarity search over everything returns the early repayment section, the superseded LEND-11 rate sheet (rev 2026-08, written as prose) and the loan-to-value section; the current table row never comes back, so the answer quotes 4.35%, which ended on 31 October. Routed by data shape, Claude calls lookup_rate with product code 5YF, 75% and today's date and gets 3.95% from LEND-11 rev 2026-11, and calls search_policy, which returns LEND-07 §8: a 1.5% fee in years 1 and 2.
exam_tip: When the answer is a row, an identifier or a number in a table, the exam wants a structured lookup or query exposed as a tool, with metadata filters such as effective date. Hybrid search is for prose. Bigger k, smaller chunks, rerankers and deleting history are distractors.
headline: Rows want lookups. Prose wants search.

concepts.t: Ask what shape the answer lives in
concepts.b: Passages, table rows, aggregates, relationships or files. Each shape has a mechanism that can produce it; similarity search over chunks suits only passages.

concepts.t: Similarity cannot find a row by its keys
concepts.b: A table row like '5YF,60.01-80.00,3.95' shares no words with 'five-year fixed at 75%'. A lookup keyed on product and band finds it every time.
Keyword (BM25) matches exact terms, semantic search matches meaning; fusing their rankings (reciprocal rank fusion) is a strong default for policy text.
Effective date, role and document type are filters in code. They pick the revision in force on the date asked, so history can stay in the library.

concepts.t: Expose each mechanism as a tool
concepts.b: Clear tool descriptions ('use for any rate figure', 'rules, not rates') let Claude route each part of a question to the right mechanism.

task_title: Evaluate connection protocols and select the appropriate integration mechanism (MCP, API/CLI, agent-to-agent)
title: Two hand-built clients, two answers: put the service behind MCP
stem: Kestrel's release-calendar service records change freezes. The CI release gate, the on-call agent and 40 engineers' Claude Code sessions all need to check it, and today each team has written its own client from its own copy of the API notes, with its own credential. Which integration mechanism should the platform team choose for the release-calendar service?

options.A: Expose the service once as an MCP server with typed tools and a server-held credential, registered in the shared .mcp.json.
options.B: Give each agent a generic HTTP tool and put the current OpenAPI specification in its context, so it can build its own requests.
options.C: Wrap the service as an autonomous agent behind an agent-to-agent protocol, so other agents delegate freeze checks to it as tasks.
options.D: Publish a small command-line tool for the service and have every agent call it through a shell tool in its own pipeline.

why: A shared internal capability that many AI hosts call is the case MCP was designed for. The platform team writes one server; every host discovers the same typed tools through tools/list; the credential stays in the server; and a change to the API is made once. Direct API or CLI calls suit a one-off scripted step one pipeline owns, and agent-to-agent protocols suit delegating a whole goal to another team's autonomous agent.

wrong.B: Every host still builds its own requests and holds a credential in context, and the specification costs tokens on every call while each copy drifts.
wrong.C: A freeze check is a typed function call, not a goal to delegate; agent-to-agent protocols are for another team's opaque autonomous agent.
wrong.D: A CLI suits a scripted step in one place; across many hosts each still wires its own shell tool, credential handling and output parsing.

fix: Write one MCP server for the shared service, register it in .mcp.json, and keep the credential in the server.
see: Bespoke clients call v1 and v2 and disagree about FRZ-118, with keys in prompts; behind one MCP server both agents find FRZ-118 and no key reaches a model.
explain: Both phases run the same two agents on the same tasks at the same moment. With each team's own client, the CI release gate follows notes written in June to the retired /v1/freeze-check endpoint, which still answers from a calendar copy last synced on 31 October, gets frozen: false and says DEPLOY into the FRZ-118 freeze, while the on-call agent's newer notes reach /v2 and find FRZ-118. A team API key and an engineer's personal token sit in the prompts and tool inputs. With one release-calendar MCP server, both agents get mcp__release-calendar__check_freeze from tools/list, the server calls v2 with its own credential, and both agents report FRZ-118.
exam_tip: Pick the mechanism by the boundary. Many AI hosts reusing one capability: MCP. One application calling a service it owns in a fixed step: direct API or CLI. Handing a goal to another organisation's autonomous agent: agent-to-agent (A2A). Subagents inside your own system are orchestration, not A2A.
headline: Many hosts, one service: one MCP server.

concepts.b: Your code decides exactly what to call. Right for a fixed workflow one application owns, such as tagging a release with an existing CLI in one pipeline.
A server exposes tools, resources and prompts over a standard protocol. Claude Code, CI agents and your own apps discover the same typed tools through tools/list.
Protocols such as A2A hand a whole task to another team's autonomous agent and get results back, without seeing its tools or reasoning.
Each hand-built copy encodes the API as it was when written. One copy calling a retired endpoint can return a stale answer that looks valid.
An MCP server holds the service credential itself, so no API key or personal token appears in a prompt, a tool input or a trace.

task_title: Evaluate progressive discovery vs. monolithic context strategy
title: 40 tools in every request: load the runbook the incident needs
stem: Kestrel's on-call agent is connected to 40 tools on seven MCP servers and a library of 24 runbooks, all loaded into every request. A typical incident uses one runbook and three or four tools, input tokens per request are well over the team's budget, and the catalogue is expected to triple next quarter. Which context strategy is best?

options.A: Keep everything loaded and turn on prompt caching for the tool definitions and runbooks, so the repeated prefix costs less on each request.
options.B: Split the agent into seven subagents, one per MCP server, each loaded with all of its own server's tools and runbooks.
options.C: Keep a small hot set of tools loaded, and let the agent search an index and load only the runbook and tools the incident needs.
options.D: Shorten every tool description and runbook to a single line, so that the whole catalogue still fits within the budget.

why: Progressive discovery keeps the request close to what the task needs: a hot set that every incident uses stays loaded, and the long tail is found through a small index and loaded on demand. The request size stops growing with the catalogue, and Claude chooses among a handful of relevant tools instead of 40. The cost is an extra search turn and the risk of a search miss, which precise names and descriptions reduce.

wrong.A: Caching lowers the price of a repeated prefix, but every request still carries all 40 tools and 24 runbooks, and the context still grows with the catalogue.
wrong.B: Incidents cross servers, so a router must still choose, and each subagent remains monolithic for its own share of the catalogue.
wrong.D: One-line descriptions and runbooks lose the steps and constraints that make tool choice and the response correct.

fix: Load a small hot set up front and let the agent search an index and load only the runbook and tools the task needs.
see: Monolithic requests carry about 8,000 input tokens each; progressive requests start with 3 tool definitions, load RB-17 and stay near 2,500, with the same correct action.
explain: Both phases handle the same incident with the same backend. Monolithic, every request carries 40 tool definitions and all 24 runbooks, about 8,000 to 9,000 input tokens per request against a 5,000-token budget, although the incident needs one runbook and four tools. Progressive, the first request carries three tool definitions (search_catalog, load, incident_note); Claude searches the index, loads RB-17, which brings flag_history, flag_disable and metrics_query, disables checkout.new-tax-engine and does not roll back the deploy. The incident costs about a third of the input tokens, and that gap widens as the catalogue grows.
exam_tip: Monolithic context fits a small, stable set of tools that every request uses. When the catalogue is large, grows, and each task uses a few items, the exam wants progressive discovery with a hot set. Caching, trimming descriptions and splitting by server do not stop context growing with the catalogue.
headline: Load the hot set. Search for the rest.

concepts.b: Every tool definition and document in the request is paid for on every turn and competes for attention. Loading things 'just in case' has a cost.
Everything up front is predictable and easy to cache, but request size grows with the catalogue and tool choice gets harder as counts pass about 30 to 50.
A one-line index is searched in code; only the runbooks and tools the task needs are loaded into the request, so its size stays close to the task.
Tools every task uses (search, load, the incident note) stay in every request. Discovery is for the long tail.
The Claude API's tool search tool defers tool definitions until searched; Agent Skills load a name and description first and the body only when triggered.

task_title: Define evaluation metrics (accuracy, latency, cost, safety, security)
title: Thumbs-up says ship, nothing cites a source: gate on a scorecard
stem: Northwind Bank's policy assistant is about to roll out to 4,000 staff. The project team proposes to approve each release when pilot users give at least 80% of answers a thumbs-up. Compliance requires every answer to cite its source and to decline questions the policy library does not cover, and finance has set a cost budget per answer. Which evaluation approach best supports the release decision?

options.A: Keep the thumbs-up rate as the release metric, but raise the bar to 95% and collect votes from a larger pilot group.
options.B: Have an LLM judge give every answer an overall quality score from 1 to 5, and release when the average reaches 4.
options.C: Score a fixed eval set on separate metrics, each with a threshold: accuracy, grounding, declines, latency and cost.
options.D: Track p95 latency and cost per answer on a dashboard, and have a compliance officer spot-check ten answers a week.

why: A release decision needs each requirement measured on its own. A scorecard over a fixed eval set gives accuracy against golden answers, citation grounding, correct declines, latency and cost per answer, each with a threshold agreed in advance, and blocks the release when any one fails. Most rows are plain code over the answers, the retrieval log and the API usage block, so the same check runs on every change. In the lab, the thumbs-up judge likes every answer while the scorecard shows that none of them cites a retrieved document.

wrong.A: A higher thumbs-up bar is still one blended proxy: staff like fluent answers whether or not they cite a source or should have declined.
wrong.B: One overall score averages properties together, so a zero on citations or declines disappears inside a good mean.
wrong.D: Latency and cost are covered, but ten spot-checks a week cannot gate a release on accuracy, grounding or declines.

fix: Score the same eval set on separate metrics, each with its own threshold, and block the release when any one fails.
see: The thumbs-up metric says release; the scorecard blocks it because no answer cites a retrieved document.
explain: The release candidate (prompt v3, tuned on pilot thumbs-up) answers five eval questions once: four in-scope questions with a golden key fact, and one the library does not cover. Phase 1 judges those answers with one metric, a thumbs-up judge, and the rate clears the 80% bar. Phase 2 scores exactly the same answers on a scorecard: accuracy against the golden facts, citation grounding (does the answer cite a document that was actually retrieved), declining the out-of-scope question, restricted chunks served to the wrong role, p95 latency and cost per answer from the usage block. Accuracy, latency and cost pass; grounding is 0 of 4, so the gate blocks the release and names what to fix. With five items the p95 is just the slowest answer: a real gate needs a few hundred items.
exam_tip: When a stem lists several requirements (cite sources, decline out-of-scope, a cost budget), the answer measures each one separately against a threshold. A satisfaction rate, an averaged judge score or a weekly spot-check is the distractor.
headline: One number hides the row that fails.

concepts.b: An eval item pairs a question with a golden answer or key fact. Code checks whether the answer contains it, so accuracy is repeatable and cheap to run on every change.
A grounded answer is supported by the retrieved text and names its source. Check that each cited document id was actually retrieved for that question.
