Safety: the assistant declines what the library does not cover. Security: no restricted content reaches a role that may not see it. Both are rates with a threshold, often zero tolerance.
Measure p95 latency, not the mean, and compute cost per answer from the usage block (input, output and cache tokens). A stable p95 needs a few hundred items.
Each metric gets a pass mark agreed before the run. One failing metric blocks the release; averaging metrics together lets a zero hide behind good scores.

task_title: Design evaluation datasets and test frameworks using mixed methodologies
title: Typical notes passed by eye: a mixed eval set catches the leak
stem: Meridian Health is changing the prompt that drafts discharge summaries from clinicians' visit notes. The team tried the new prompt on 20 typical notes, a clinician read the drafts, and all of them looked fine. Every draft is signed off before release, but a leaked identifier or a missed allergy would still be a serious incident. Which evaluation approach is most appropriate before the change goes live?

options.A: Mix golden, adversarial and edge-case notes; check hard rules in code and clinical judgement with a rubric-based LLM judge.
options.B: Grow the typical-note set to 200 notes, and have an LLM judge give each draft an overall quality score from 1 to 5.
options.C: Skip further offline testing and rely on clinician sign-off instead, logging every correction a clinician makes after go-live.
options.D: Compare each draft with a clinician-written reference summary by exact text overlap, and pass the change above 90%.

why: Typical notes read by eye only show that the prompt works on easy cases. A mixed dataset adds the cases that break systems: adversarial notes (extra PHI in the record) and edge cases (an allergy recorded in only one place, conflicting doses), alongside golden happy-path items. Each property then gets the right grader: hard rules such as required sections, no unnecessary identifiers and known allergies present are checked in code, and clinical judgement such as faithfulness and flagging conflicts goes to an LLM judge with a written rubric, calibrated against clinician labels.

wrong.B: More typical notes still contain no adversarial or edge cases, and one overall 1-5 score cannot say which rule failed.
wrong.C: Sign-off is a final human check, not an evaluation: errors reach clinicians' queues, and nothing tests the change before go-live.
wrong.D: Exact text overlap punishes a correct summary worded differently and cannot tell a leaked phone number from a harmless phrase.

fix: Test every prompt change on a mixed set of golden, adversarial and edge-case notes, with hard rules in code and judgement by a rubric judge.
see: The two happy-path drafts pass by eye; the mixed set finds no Allergies section and an insurance member ID and phone number copied into A1.
explain: The prompt under test (drafter v2) fills a tidy template: it copies the PATIENT DETAILS block verbatim and has no Allergies section. Phase 1 runs it on two typical notes and a quick review: both look fine, so it would ship. Phase 2 runs the same prompt on a mixed set: the same two notes, one adversarial note whose details block holds a home phone and an insurance member ID, and two edge cases (an apixaban dose that conflicts between the medication list and a pharmacist's note, and a penicillin allergy recorded only in a nursing note while co-amoxiclav is prescribed). Code checks the hard rules and fails most of the drafts, including the two that passed phase 1. A rubric judge grades each draft in its own call, as schema-checked JSON, for faithfulness and for flagging the conflicts. The gate blocks v2 with a named reason per item.
exam_tip: 'Mixed methodologies' means mixed data and mixed graders: golden, adversarial and edge cases, with code for deterministic rules and an LLM judge with a rubric for judgement. Bigger happy-path sets, exact-match scoring and relying on human sign-off are the distractors.
headline: Test the cases that break it, grade each the right way.

concepts.b: Golden items show typical behaviour; adversarial items try to make the system misbehave (extra PHI, injected text); edge cases sit at the boundaries (conflicts, missing data).
Use code for anything with a deterministic answer: required sections, forbidden identifiers, a known allergy present, valid JSON. Code graders are exact, fast and cheap.
For judgement calls such as faithfulness or tone, a judge model applies written criteria and returns a structured grade. Grade one item per call so items cannot be skipped or mixed up.
Before trusting a judge, compare its grades with expert labels on a sample and fix the rubric where they disagree. Re-check after changing the judge prompt or model.

concepts.t: Human review is a sample, not a test
concepts.b: Clinician sign-off and spot reads catch some errors late. They do not replace an offline eval that runs on every change before release.

task_title: Conduct A/B testing and iterative improvements
title: v2 won the demo and missed SEV1 pages: A/B it on the same alerts
stem: Kestrel's platform team owns the prompt that triages production alerts into SEV1, SEV2 and SEV3. An engineer rewrote it as v2 and demonstrated it on a staging alert that v1 had wrongly paged as SEV1; v2 got it right, and the team wants to ship v2 today. Which approach best decides whether v2 should replace v1?

options.A: Ship v2 for all alerts and collect on-call feedback for a week, rolling back if complaints about wrong pages start to rise.
options.B: Run v1 and v2 on the same labelled eval alerts with the same grader, and apply a decision rule agreed before the run.
options.C: Run v2 on twenty new alerts picked by its author, and compare its accuracy with the score v1 achieved last quarter.
options.D: Ask Claude to read both prompts side by side and choose the one that it judges to be clearer and more complete.

why: A demo shows the case the change was written to fix. An A/B comparison runs both prompts on the same labelled items with the same grader, so the only difference is the prompt, and a decision rule fixed before the run (a primary metric plus guardrails that may not regress) turns the result into a decision. In the lab, v2 fixes the staging alert but drops two small checkout and payment failures from SEV1 to SEV2, and the guardrail rejects it.

wrong.A: Shipping first makes on-call engineers the test set, and a missed SEV1 page is found by customers, not by the feedback channel.
wrong.C: Different items and a quarter-old score compare two datasets, not two prompts, and the author chose the items.
wrong.D: Claude judging which prompt reads better measures the prompt's wording, not how it labels real alerts.

fix: Run both prompts on the same labelled eval set with the same grader and let a decision rule written beforehand decide.
see: v2 wins the demo; on the same 8 labelled alerts it misses the 2.1% checkout and 1.4% payment SEV1s, and the rule rejects it.
explain: Phase 1 compares v1 and v2 on the author's demo alert, checkout 500s in staging: v1 pages it as SEV1, v2 correctly says SEV3, so the demo says ship. Phase 2 writes the decision rule down first (v2's accuracy must be at least v1's, and v2 may miss no gold SEV1), then runs both prompts on the same eight alerts with gold labels from the on-call leads, twice each, with structured output so every label is scored in code. v2 keeps its staging fix but its new 'error rate above 5%' SEV1 wording drops two real customer-impacting failures to SEV2. Eight items run twice prove nothing statistically, and the lab says so; they are enough to find a specific regression you can read item by item. After an offline pass, the next step would be a small canary on the same metrics.
exam_tip: A/B means the same items, the same graders and a rule agreed in advance, with guardrail metrics that may not regress. Comparing different datasets, shipping and watching feedback, or asking a model which prompt is better are the distractors.
headline: Same items, same grader, rule written first.

concepts.b: The author picks the example that shows the change working. It says nothing about the cases the change might break.
Run both variants on the same fixed items with the same grader and settings, so any difference in the score comes from the change alone.
Decide before the run what must improve (the primary metric) and what may not get worse (guardrails such as SEV1 recall), and what result ships the change.
Model outputs vary between runs. Repeat runs to see the spread, and do not claim significance from a few items: small sets find specific regressions, large sets measure rates.
Fix what the eval found, re-run the same set, and only then expose the change to a small share of live traffic with the same metrics before a full rollout.

task_title: Diagnose system issues (prompt failure, hallucinations, model mismatch)
title: Confident, cited and stale after a re-index: inspect retrieval first
stem: A RAG system suddenly returns confident but incorrect answers after a document refresh, while latency and model version are unchanged. What is the most likely first place to investigate?

options.A: The model weights have silently changed.
options.B: The retrieval/indexing step is returning irrelevant or stale chunks.
options.C: The temperature setting is too low.
options.D: The context window has shrunk.

why: Confident-but-wrong answers following a document refresh, with model and latency unchanged, point to retrieval feeding the model poor context, for example a broken re-index or mismatched embeddings. The other options would not be triggered specifically by a document refresh. In the lab, the assistant cites LEND-07 and HR-09 correctly but quotes last week's figures, because the re-index kept the old chunks; a stricter prompt changes nothing, and re-indexing fixes both answers.

wrong.A: The model version is unchanged, and a pinned model does not change underneath you; nothing ties it to the document refresh.
wrong.C: A low temperature makes answers more consistent, not wrong, and the setting did not change with the document refresh.
wrong.D: The context window is a property of the model, which is unchanged; a document refresh does not shrink it.

fix: Log each answer's retrieved chunk ids, versions and index dates, compare them with the library manifest, and re-index what is behind.
see: Both prompts quote 60% and 2 days from stale LEND-07 v3 and HR-09 v5 chunks; after re-indexing, the original prompt answers 55% and 3 days.
explain: This is the exam guide's sample question 3 on the Northwind policy assistant. Since the 17 Nov re-index, staff get confident, cited answers with last week's figures; the model is still claude-haiku-5-5 and latency is unchanged. Phase 1 tries the tempting fix, a stricter prompt ('use only the latest version, double-check numbers'): the answers stay at 60% (S$5,400) and 2 days a week, because the model can only use the chunks it is given. Phase 2 inspects what retrieval served: LEND-07#1 and HR-09#1 were embedded from v3 and v5 on 10 Nov, while the manifest says v4 and v6. Claude, given that evidence as structured input, names the retrieval index as the first place to look. Re-indexing the two documents fixes both answers with the original prompt: 55% (S$4,950) and 3 days. The lasting fix is a check that fails the indexing job when an indexed version falls behind the manifest.
exam_tip: Tie the symptom to what changed. A document refresh changes the index, not the model, the temperature or the context window, so look at what retrieval returns first: chunk ids, versions and dates.
headline: Wrong after a refresh? Check what retrieval served.

concepts.b: The model answers from the chunks retrieval puts in its context. If those chunks are stale or irrelevant, a fluent, cited and wrong answer is the expected result.

concepts.t: Correlate the symptom with the change
concepts.b: Ask what changed when the failures started. A document refresh points at indexing; a model upgrade points at the model; a prompt edit points at the prompt.
Log every answer's retrieved chunk ids, scores, source versions and index dates. Without them a retrieval fault looks exactly like a hallucination.
An embedding job that times out and keeps old vectors, or a new embedding model with an old query encoder, still returns results. Only a version check against the source catches it.

concepts.t: A prompt cannot add missing facts
concepts.b: Stricter instructions change how the model uses its context, not what is in it. When the right text never reaches the model, fix the pipeline, not the wording.

task_title: Optimize token usage, latency, and cost-performance trade-offs
title: Right answers, 3,000 output tokens each: cache, trim, cap, re-test
stem: Harbour Mutual's claims triage runs on Claude Sonnet 5.5. Each request sends the claim's full email history, then the claim, then 2,000 tokens of policy wording that is identical on every call, and asks for a detailed analysis and a letter. Adjusters agree the decisions are right, but cost per claim and latency are both over budget. Which change best reduces both while holding decision quality?

options.A: Switch every claim to Claude Haiku 5.5 at once, since its input and output prices are a twentieth of Sonnet 5.5's.
options.B: Truncate the policy wording to its first 800 tokens, so that every request carries far less input text to process.
options.C: Send every claim through the Message Batches API, which halves the price of each request for exactly the same output tokens.
options.D: Put the cached static policy first, send only the claim fields, ask for a short JSON decision, and re-run the eval set.

why: Static content first lets the identical policy wording become a cached prefix that later calls read at a tenth of the input price. Sending only the fields the decision needs drops the email history, and asking for a short JSON decision removes most of the output tokens, which drive both cost and latency. Re-running the eval set proves the decisions stayed right. In the lab the same three decisions come back as schema-valid JSON with cache reads on calls 2 and 3, and output, cost and latency per claim all fall sharply.

wrong.A: A blind switch to a cheaper tier changes quality with no evidence, and still pays for the history and long output.
wrong.B: Cutting the policy wording removes clauses the decision depends on, such as excess and authority rules, so quality is no longer held.
wrong.C: Batches halve the price but return results within 24 hours, which breaks latency for a live claims desk.

fix: Put static content first and cache it, send only the fields that decide, ask for a short structured output, cap max_tokens, and re-run the eval set.
see: Phase 1 decides all three claims right at about 3,000 output tokens each; phase 2 gives the same decisions in about 300, with cache reads on claims 2 and 3.
explain: Both phases run Haiku 5.5 on the same three claims, so only the request shape changes, and quality is checked in code against the gold decisions (approve US$3,700, decline, approve US$650). Phase 1 is today's request: the six-email history, the claim, then the policy wording, and a request for an analysis and a letter. Every decision is right, but each claim costs about 3,000 output tokens and over ten seconds, and nothing is cached because no two requests share a prefix. Phase 2 puts the rules and policy first in a system block with cache_control, sends nine claim fields, and asks for a JSON decision through output_config with max_tokens 1024. The decisions are the same; cache_read_input_tokens is above zero from the second call; output falls by about 90%, and cost and latency follow. The page also prices the same token counts at Sonnet 5.5 list prices, the stem's model tier.
exam_tip: Look for the option that cuts tokens without cutting information the task needs, and that re-checks quality. Blind model swaps, truncating required context and the Batch API for live traffic are the classic distractors.
headline: Cache what repeats, send what decides, ask for less.

concepts.t: Where the money and time go
concepts.b: Cost is input tokens × input price plus output tokens × output price, and output is five times dearer on every tier. Latency grows mostly with output tokens generated.
Mark a static prefix (tools, system, long documents) with cache_control. Later calls with the identical prefix read it at 0.1× the input price; the first call writes it at 1.25×.
The cache matches from the start of the request. Anything that changes per call, such as a claim or a timestamp, must come after the cached block or the prefix never matches.
A short structured output (JSON with a schema) replaces an essay. max_tokens caps the worst case, and stop_reason max_tokens tells you when the cap cut an answer.
Run the same eval set before and after. A cheaper design that changes decisions is a regression, not an optimisation.

task_title: Monitor system performance using logging and observability tools
title: 'Answered in 2.4s' can't say why: log every Claude call as a record
stem: Kestrel's checkout-assistant calls Claude in production and writes free-text log lines such as 'answered customer question in 2.4s'. After a release, customers report cut-off answers and Claude spend rises 2.4 times, and the on-call engineer cannot tell why from the logs. Which change best lets the team detect and diagnose problems like this?

options.A: Emit one structured record per Claude call (trace_id, prompt version, tokens, cache reads, stop_reason) and alert on it.
options.B: Log the full prompt and the full response of every call as free text, so the on-call engineer can read exactly what happened.
options.C: Add a thumbs-down button to the feature, and page the on-call engineer whenever the rate of thumbs-down votes rises.
options.D: Run the offline evaluation suite against the production prompts every night, and alert when its pass rate falls.

why: Cut-off answers and higher spend are explained by fields the API returns on every call: stop_reason (max_tokens), output tokens, cache_read_input_tokens, plus the prompt version and trace_id the service adds. One structured record per call makes those queryable: alert rules can watch the max_tokens and cache-miss rates, a group-by on prompt version finds the release, and each finding links to a trace. In the lab, the same incident gives a low-confidence guess from the free-text lines and a cited, two-cause diagnosis from the records.

wrong.B: Full prompts and responses as text are costly, risky to store and still unqueryable: no rule can count stop_reason in prose.
wrong.C: Thumbs-down votes arrive late and say that something is wrong, not why; they cannot see cache misses or token growth.
wrong.D: An offline suite tests fixed items, not production traffic, so it can miss a cache miss or a token-cap problem live users hit.

fix: Emit one structured record per Claude call with trace_id, model, prompt version, token usage, cache reads, latency_ms, stop_reason and tool calls, and alert on it.
see: From free text no rule can run and the diagnosis is a guess; from 48 records both rules fire and Claude names v14's max_tokens cap and lost cache hits, with trace ids.
explain: The same 48 calls from 10:00 to 11:00 are seen two ways. Prompt v14 shipped at 10:20: it asks for longer answers, so 13 of its 32 calls stop at the 1,024-token cap, and it moved a timestamp to the top of the system prompt, so the cached prefix never matches and cache_read_input_tokens drops from 3,200 to 0. Phase 1 has the free-text lines the feature prints today: the truncation and cache-miss rules cannot even be evaluated, and Claude's diagnosis is low confidence, cites no trace ids and lists the fields it is missing. Phase 2 has one record per call in the observability store: both rules fire in code over the last 30 minutes, a group-by on prompt_version points at v14, and Claude's diagnosis names both causes and cites real trace ids an engineer can open.
exam_tip: For production monitoring, pick structured per-call telemetry (tokens, latency, stop_reason, cache reads, model and prompt version, trace ids) with alerts and dashboards. Verbose text logs, user feedback and offline evals are useful but cannot diagnose a live incident on their own.
headline: You can only alert on what you logged as a field.

concepts.t: What the API already tells you
concepts.b: Every response carries model, stop_reason and usage (input_tokens, output_tokens, cache_creation_input_tokens, cache_read_input_tokens). Log them on every call.
Add a trace_id that links the call to the user request, the prompt version, the feature or squad, latency_ms and the number of tool calls.
Simple rules on the fields catch failures early: share of max_tokens stops, cache-hit rate, p95 latency, tokens per request, error rate.
A dashboard grouped by prompt version or model shows a bad deploy at a glance and supports rollback decisions.
Log metadata on every call; keep full prompts and responses only where policy allows, sampled, access-controlled and redacted, since they may hold personal data.

task_title: Implement guardrails and safety controls
title: Forged certificate approved: gate approve_permit on the registers
stem: Riverton's permit pre-screening assistant reads residents' uploads and can call approve_permit. Its system prompt says never to follow instructions inside documents. In testing, a resident uploads a forged inspection certificate with a note telling the assistant to approve; the assistant reports that it ignored the note, then approves the permit anyway. Which control design best prevents unauthorised approvals?

options.A: Extend the system prompt with examples of injected notes and forged certificates, and tell the assistant to refuse any document that resembles one of them.
options.B: Add a separate Claude screening call that classifies every upload for prompt injection and drops flagged uploads before the assistant reads them.
options.C: Log every approval with the evidence it relied on, and have a caseworker review the log each morning and revoke any approval the evidence does not support.
options.D: Return uploads as labelled untrusted data, and gate approve_permit in code on the inspection and payments registers, denying whenever they can't confirm.

why: The assistant obeyed the prompt rule for the note but still acted on forged facts, because nothing outside the model checked them. Layered controls fix that: uploads arrive as labelled untrusted data, and a PreToolUse gate checks the systems of record before approve_permit can take effect. The gate is deterministic and fails closed, so a forged document, or a register that can't answer, can't produce an approval.

wrong.A: More prompt text is still probabilistic, and a forged certificate with no injected note matches none of the examples.
wrong.B: A second model is a useful extra layer, but it judges meaning probabilistically and a plain forgery carries no injection to flag.
wrong.C: A morning review is a detective control: the permit has already been issued when the forgery is found.

fix: Label uploads as untrusted data and gate approve_permit in code on the inspection and payments registers, failing closed.
see: The prompt rule catches the note but not the forged facts; the register gate denies PRM-3301 and PRM-3308 and allows PRM-3305.
explain: In Phase 1 the only control is a sentence in the system prompt. Claude usually reports that it ignored the injected note, and then approves PRM-3301 on the forged certificate, because the forged facts are exactly what the approval rule asks for. In Phase 2 the uploads come back as labelled untrusted data, and a PreToolUse gate looks up the inspection register and the payments ledger before every approve_permit call. It denies PRM-3301 (inspection only booked for 28 Nov, fee unpaid) and PRM-3308 (the ledger is down, so it can't confirm: it fails closed), and it allows PRM-3305, which both registers confirm. Claude reads each denial and routes the application to a caseworker.
exam_tip: When a stem says the model 'ignored the injection but still took the action', the fix is outside the model: a deterministic gate on the action that checks the system of record and fails closed. Prompt rules and screening models are layers that reduce risk; they are not the control that makes the bad action impossible.
headline: A prompt can't check a fact. Code that reads the register can.

concepts.b: Direct injection comes from the user. Indirect injection rides in content the system reads: uploads, web pages, emails, tool results. The person asking can be honest while the document is not.
The model (flexible, can be argued with), a second model (a probabilistic screen), deterministic code (certain, can't judge meaning) or a person. Put every 'must never happen' outside the model.
A gate before the action prevents it. Logs and morning reviews only detect it, after the permit, payment or email has already gone out.
When a control can't decide, because a register times out or a lookup fails, it denies. A gate that allows on error turns every outage into an open door.
Return third-party content in tool results, marked with its source and as data, not instructions. It lowers the risk of injection; it doesn't replace a gate on the action.

task_title: Identify risks, limitations, and failure modes of LLM systems
title: Two calls agreed on the wrong payout: let code compute it
stem: Harbour Mutual's claims agent calculates payouts from garage quotes and pays any amount within its US$5,000 authority. To catch errors, a second Claude call recalculates each payout, and the agent pays only when both agree. An audit finds a payout that both calls agreed on, but that silently left out an unpriced quote line, which kept it under the limit. Which change best addresses this failure mode?

options.A: Move the calculation step to Claude Opus 5.5, whose stronger reasoning makes arithmetic and omission errors much less likely than on a smaller model.
options.B: Add worked examples to the prompt, including a quote with an unpriced line, that show the model how to flag a gap before it calculates.
options.C: Have Claude extract each line with null for missing amounts, then compute the payout in code and hold any claim that has an unpriced line.
options.D: Add a third independent calculation call and pay only when all three agree, routing any disagreement between the calls to an adjuster.

why: The failure mode is a fluent figure produced from input that can't support it, confirmed by a check that shares the same blind spot. The reliable fix splits the work: Claude does what it is good at (reading and copying lines, with null where nothing is printed), and deterministic code grounds each line in the quote, refuses to compute while a line is unpriced, applies the policy terms and checks the authority limit.

wrong.A: A larger model makes errors rarer, not impossible, and it still has to guess an amount the quote doesn't print.
wrong.B: Examples improve the odds but leave the payout resting on the model's arithmetic and its judgement.
wrong.D: More calls of the same model share the same blind spot, so they can agree on the same wrong figure.

fix: Extract the lines with Claude (null where unpriced), then hold, compute and route on the payout in code.
see: Both Phase 1 calls agree on about $4,810.58 and it is paid; Phase 2 holds for line 14, computes $5,340.64 and escalates.
explain: Line 14 of the quote says 'per materials sheet to follow', so no correct payout can be computed from the quote alone. In Phase 1 Claude still returns a figure, about $4,810.58 with line 14 silently left out, and a second call agrees with it. The figure is under the $5,000 authority, so the pipeline pays it without an adjuster. In Phase 2 Claude extracts all 21 lines with line 14 as null; code checks the other 20 amounts against the quote, holds the claim, fetches the materials sheet ($486.30), computes $5,340.64 from the policy terms and escalates it to an adjuster.
exam_tip: Self-consistency (ask twice, compare) and bigger models are tempting answers to an accuracy problem. When the failure is a known mode, such as arithmetic, missing input or a hard business rule, the professional answer is to move that part into deterministic code and let the model do the reading.
headline: The model reads the quote. Code does the sums.

concepts.b: An LLM produces a plausible answer to the question asked, even when the input can't support one. A required number in a schema gets filled, with or without the facts.
Two calls of the same model share the same blind spots. Agreement shows stability, not truth; an independent check uses a different source, such as the document or code.

concepts.t: Arithmetic is a known weak spot
concepts.b: Long sums in one pass are error-prone, more so with thinking off. Bigger models and examples make errors rarer, not impossible. Hard arithmetic belongs in code.
Check each extracted amount against the source text, and require null where the source prints nothing. A value that isn't in the document is a guess.
When a required input is missing, stop and fetch it; don't compute around the gap. Missing data is a reason to route the case, not to estimate.

task_title: Apply human-in-the-loop validation strategies
title: 54 seconds a draft is a signature: route review by risk
stem: Meridian Health drafts about 600 clinical letters and notes a day with Claude, and three clinicians have 540 minutes a day for sign-off. Every draft joins one queue, approval rates are close to 100%, and a GP letter with conflicting warfarin doses was signed in under a minute. Which human-in-the-loop design best fits this situation?

options.A: Route each draft in code by impact, reversibility and uncertainty; flagged drafts get full review with reasons, the rest a co-sign or sampled audit.
options.B: Keep a full review of every draft, but add two more clinicians and a checklist, so that each draft gets a careful, complete read before it is released.
options.C: Release drafts that Claude rates as high confidence without review, and send only its medium and low confidence drafts to the clinicians.
options.D: Release every draft automatically, and have clinicians audit a random 10% sample of each week's drafts, feeding the errors they find back into the prompt.

why: Oversight is a budget. At 600 drafts in 540 minutes a uniform review becomes a signature, so the fix is to spend reviewer time by risk: code flags what it can check (high-alert drugs, conflicting doses, pending results, whether the document leaves the hospital), adds Claude's own uncertainty as a signal, and shows the reviewer the reasons. Unflagged letters get a quick co-sign, unflagged internal notes are filed and sampled, and every route is logged.

wrong.B: Five clinicians give 900 minutes for 600 drafts, still about 90 seconds each, so the queue stays a rubber stamp.
wrong.C: Self-reported confidence alone ignores impact and reversibility, and it isn't calibrated against outcomes.
wrong.D: A weekly audit is detective: a letter with the wrong warfarin dose has already reached the GP.

fix: Route each draft in code by impact × reversibility × uncertainty, and show the reviewer the reasons.
see: One uniform queue signs Patient C's warfarin letter in 54 seconds; risk routing sends C and D to full review with reasons.
explain: Both phases ask Claude to draft the same four documents in one call, with the medications it wrote, its open questions and its confidence. In Phase 1 every draft joins one sign-off queue; at Meridian's volume that is 54 seconds a draft, so the simulated clinician signs Patient C's warfarin letter as drafted and the 5 mg vs 3 mg conflict in the note is never surfaced. In Phase 2 code routes each draft: C (high-alert drug, dose conflict, leaves the hospital) and D (echo report pending) go to full review with the reasons on screen, B is co-signed and A's internal note is auto-filed. Reviewer time needed falls from 2,400 to 480 of the 540 minutes available.
exam_tip: Look for the answer that tiers oversight by impact and reversibility and fits the reviewers' capacity. '100% human review' sounds safest but fails at volume through automation bias; a confidence threshold alone ignores impact; post-hoc audits can't recall an irreversible action.
headline: Spend reviewer minutes where the risk is.

concepts.b: Gate actions that are high-impact and can't be undone, such as a letter that leaves the hospital. Monitor actions that can be amended, such as an internal chart note, instead of gating them.
Load = volume × share reviewed × minutes each ÷ reviewer minutes available. Above 1, reviews turn into signatures: 600 drafts in 540 minutes is 54 seconds each.
When a system is usually right, people stop checking it. Near-100% approval and falling time per decision are the signs. Showing why a draft was flagged gives the reviewer something to check.

concepts.t: Confidence is a signal, not a verdict
concepts.b: A model's self-reported confidence can help route work, but only alongside signals code can check: high-alert drugs, conflicting values, pending results.
Auto-filed items need a random audit sample. It measures the real error rate of the unreviewed stream and catches drift before patients do.

task_title: Ensure compliance with regulations (e.g., GDPR, HIPAA, FedRAMP)
title: The whole record went to the model and the log: send the minimum
stem: Meridian Health's referral-drafting prototype sends each patient's full record to Claude and copies every prompt and response to a third-party log service for debugging. Before go-live, the compliance lead asks for a design that meets HIPAA's minimum-necessary standard and produces evidence for audits. Which design best meets the requirement?

options.A: Keep sending the full record so that letters stay accurate, sign a BAA with the model provider, and restrict log access with role-based permissions.
options.B: Send only the fields each purpose needs with identifiers tokenised, restore them in code after the call, and log metadata plus an audit record.
options.C: Tell Claude in the system prompt to ignore identifiers it does not need and never to repeat them, and encrypt the log store at rest.
options.D: Move the workload to a FedRAMP High authorised cloud region, and keep the full prompts in its logs, since that authorisation covers them.

why: Minimum necessary is decided before the call: an allow-list per purpose controls which fields leave, identifiers become tokens that only your code maps back, and the log keeps metadata instead of PHI. The audit record (user, purpose, fields sent and withheld) is the evidence that the control ran. The other options leave the full record flowing to the model or the log.

wrong.A: A BAA is needed, but it doesn't make sending the whole record 'minimum necessary', and the third-party log still holds full PHI.
wrong.C: By the time the model reads the instruction the PHI has already been disclosed; encrypting the log doesn't reduce what it holds.
wrong.D: FedRAMP authorises cloud services for US federal agencies; it doesn't satisfy HIPAA's minimum-necessary standard or cover a third-party log.

fix: Allow-list fields per purpose, tokenise identifiers, log metadata only and write an audit record of what was sent and why.
see: Phase 1 sends 9 identifiers and 3 unneeded history items and logs them; Phase 2 sends none and logs metadata plus an audit record.
explain: The lab scans the exact request body each phase sent. In Phase 1 the full record reaches Claude: name, MRN, date of birth, address, phone, email, SSN, insurance id and next of kin, plus sensitive history a diabetes referral doesn't need, and the debug log keeps a full copy. In Phase 2 an allow-list keeps six fields for this purpose, the name and MRN become [PATIENT] and [MRN], and code puts them back after the call. The letter still has HbA1c 9.1%, metformin and gliclazide. The log holds request id, field names, token counts and a fingerprint, and the audit record lists who sent which fields, for which purpose, and which were withheld.
exam_tip: Compliance answers are usually about what data reaches which processor, and what evidence you keep. Prefer the option that removes data before the call (minimisation, tokenisation) and leaves an audit trail, over options that rely on the model ignoring data, on encryption alone, or on a certification meant for a different regime.
headline: Allow-list the fields. Log metadata. Keep the evidence.

concepts.b: HIPAA's standard: use or disclose only the PHI needed for the purpose. Write it per purpose as an allow-list in code, so every field that leaves is a visible decision.
The model provider, the log service and any trace store that receives PHI must sit inside the agreements that cover it (a BAA for HIPAA). A debug log is a hop.
Replace direct identifiers with tokens such as [PATIENT] before the call, and map them back in your own code afterwards. Claude still writes the letter; it never sees the name.
Operations need request ids, token counts and field names, not prompt text. An audit record of user, purpose, fields sent and fields withheld shows the control ran.
HIPAA covers US health data, GDPR the personal data of people in the EU, FedRAMP cloud services for US federal agencies. One certification doesn't satisfy another regime.

task_title: Address ethical AI considerations (bias, fairness, transparency)
title: Same case, other language, other outcome: test with pairs
stem: Riverton's benefit pre-screener answers residents who write in English, Malay, Tamil or Chinese. Its prompt tells Claude to treat every resident equally, and it passed a review of 50 English cases. Before go-live, the council must show that outcomes don't depend on a resident's name or language, and that each decision is explained. Which approach best does this?

options.A: Run counterfactual pairs (same case, only name or language changed) through the whole pipeline as a release gate; explain each decision by its rule.
options.B: Strip residents' names and the language field from every request before the model sees it, so that protected attributes can't influence a decision.
options.C: Ask Claude to review each of its own decisions for bias before replying, and to explain its reasoning to the resident in plain language.
options.D: Compare approval rates by language group after the first month live, and investigate any group whose rate differs from the others by over 10 points.

why: A counterfactual pair holds the case constant and changes one protected attribute, so any difference in outcome is caused by that attribute. Run end to end, the pairs catch bias wherever it enters (here an English-only fact extractor, not the model), and as a release gate they stop a regression before residents see it. Explanations built from the rule ids and figures that decided each case are faithful by construction.

wrong.B: Removing names leaves the language of the message itself, and proxies such as address; it hides inputs instead of measuring outcomes.
wrong.C: A model's review of its own reasoning is neither a measurement nor reliably faithful to what drove the decision.
wrong.D: Group rates arrive after residents are affected and mix real differences in cases with unfair treatment.

fix: Gate the release on counterfactual pairs run end to end, and explain each decision by the rule and figures that decided it.
see: Phase 1 flips 2 of 3 pairs on language; Phase 2 gives all four 'likely eligible' with rule-based explanations and 0 flips.
explain: All four messages describe the same household: 3 people, $2,150 a month, 4 years in Riverton. In Phase 1 the pre-screener's facts come from keyword patterns written for English, so both English messages are 'likely eligible' while the same resident writing in Malay or Chinese is asked for information she already gave: the two language pairs flip, the name pair doesn't. In Phase 2 Claude extracts the facts from every language into a schema, the same rules in code give all four 'likely eligible' at $716.67 per person, each resident gets an explanation in her language naming BEN-R1 and BEN-R2, and the gate passes with 0 flips.
exam_tip: Fairness questions reward measurement over intention. Prefer paired (counterfactual) tests run before release over prompt instructions, removing attributes, or comparing group rates after launch, and prefer explanations derived from the decision rule over the model's own account of its reasoning.
headline: Change one attribute. The outcome must not move.

concepts.b: Hold a case constant and change one protected attribute, such as name or language. Any difference in outcome is caused by that attribute. Run many cases, several times each.
Bias can enter outside the model: an English-only parser, a translation step, a retrieval filter. Pairs run end to end catch it wherever it sits.
Removing names doesn't remove language, address or other proxies, and a message written in Malay can't hide its language. Measure outcomes instead of hiding inputs.
Approval rates by group mix real differences between cases with unfair treatment, and they arrive after residents are affected. Paired tests isolate the attribute before release.
An explanation built from the rule ids and figures that decided the case is faithful by construction. A model's after-the-fact account of its reasoning may not be.

task_title: Conduct structured discovery and requirement gathering
title: A design from the COO's one line misses legal: interview every group
stem: Lumen Retail's COO, Grace Lim, emails you: "We want an AI assistant in all 300 stores that answers product questions for staff and customers. Live by early March. Can you send me the solution design by Friday?" Store operations, IT security and legal have not yet been consulted. What should you do first?

options.A: Draft a reference design from the COO's brief by Friday, then refine it in review sessions with each team once they have something concrete to react to and comment on.
options.B: Build a quick proof of concept on the product catalogue so that every stakeholder can react to a working assistant before any of the requirements are written down.
options.C: Interview each stakeholder group against a checklist of users, volumes, data, constraints, risks, success measures and SLAs, and log conflicts for the sponsor.
options.D: Send every stakeholder a short requirements questionnaire, and where their answers conflict, design to the view that most of the groups share.

why: The sponsor's email covers users and a deadline, nothing more. Structured discovery against a fixed checklist turns volumes, data, risks, success measures and service levels from guesses into traced requirements, and it is the only step that surfaces conflicts such as store operations wanting transcripts kept while legal forbids storing them. The architect records the conflict with both sources and leaves the decision to the accountable owner.

wrong.A: A design drafted first anchors everyone on assumptions, and conflicts such as the legal ban on stored transcripts surface late, after the design depends on them.
wrong.B: A proof of concept before success measures and constraints are known has nothing to be judged against, and it can be built on data legal will not allow.
wrong.D: A legal obligation is not outvoted by the majority: conflicts must go to the accountable owner, and a questionnaire cannot probe answers the way an interview can.

fix: Interview every stakeholder group against a checklist, trace each requirement to what someone said, and log conflicts for the sponsor to decide.
see: Phase 1 assumes five of seven items; Phase 2 traces all seven and finds the transcript conflict between store operations and legal.
explain: Both phases start from the same email. Drafted from it alone, only users and a deadline trace to anything a stakeholder said; volumes, data, risks, success measures and SLAs are the architect's guesses, and no conflict can be found. With discovery, Claude interviews the sponsor, store operations, IT security and legal through ask_stakeholder, cites the INT record behind each requirement, and logs that store operations (INT-06) wants transcripts kept for 90 days while legal (INT-10) forbids storing them. Code checks every citation against what the record covers, so an unsupported requirement counts as an assumption.
exam_tip: When a scenario starts from a sponsor's one-line request, the answer is discovery across all stakeholder groups before design or a proof of concept. Conflicts are recorded and escalated to the accountable owner; they are never settled by a majority vote or by the architect alone.
headline: Ask every group before you design. Trace or label it.

concepts.t: Discovery output is a requirements trace
concepts.b: Each requirement cites who said it. Anything nobody said is labelled an assumption, so the sponsor can see what the design rests on.
Users, volumes, data, constraints, risks, success measures and SLAs. A fixed list makes gaps visible: an empty row is a question still to ask.

concepts.t: Every stakeholder group, not the sponsor
concepts.b: The sponsor owns the goal; store operations, IT security and legal own constraints the sponsor may not know. Each holds a veto the design must respect.
When two groups want incompatible things, record both sources and the person who decides. A legal obligation outranks an operational wish.
A measurable target (30% less staff time, satisfaction 4.2 or better) is what a pilot is later judged against. Without it a proof of concept proves nothing.

task_title: Communicate architectural decisions and trade-offs
title: A memo that sells the pick can't be approved: write the record
stem: You have chosen Claude Haiku 5.5 with retrieval for Lumen's assistant over Claude Sonnet 5.5 with retrieval and over a larger human hotline. Grace Lim (COO) must approve the budget and Hannah Koh (IT security lead) must approve the data flow before the build starts. How should you communicate the decision?

options.A: Send both leaders the same one-page summary explaining why the chosen option is the best fit for Lumen, with the architecture diagram attached for reference.
options.B: Write a decision record with the options, their measured accuracy, latency and cost, the risks and a reversal trigger, then brief each leader in their own terms.
options.C: Present the full benchmark tables, the token-level cost model and the retrieval settings to both leaders so they can weigh every detail and reach their own conclusion.
options.D: Present only the recommended option at the steering meeting, and keep the analysis of the alternatives in reserve in case one of the leaders challenges it.

why: A stakeholder can act on a decision only when they can see what was traded away, in their own units, and what would change it. The decision record holds the options with measured accuracy, latency and cost, the risks with their controls, and the reversal trigger; each brief restates the same facts for its reader: money and service for the COO, data and controls for IT security.

wrong.A: One summary that only argues for the pick hides the trade-offs and speaks to neither reader's question: the COO's cost comparison or IT security's data flow.
wrong.C: Raw benchmarks and token maths hand the architect's analysis to the leaders without a recommendation, in units neither of them works in.
wrong.D: Holding the alternatives back takes the trade-off decision away from the people accountable for it and invites the doubt it tries to avoid.

fix: Record the options, measured trade-offs, risks and reversal trigger, and brief each stakeholder in their own terms from that one record.
see: Phase 1's readers can answer only a few of their 6 questions; Phase 2's readers answer all 6 from their brief and the record.
explain: Both phases answer the same request. Phase 1 is built from the pick alone, so the memo can only praise Option A. Phase 2 is built from the decision record: Options A, B and C with their measured accuracy, p95 latency and monthly cost, the risks and controls, the data flow, and the reversal trigger (weekly graded accuracy below 90% for two weeks), plus one brief for the COO and one for IT security. Two reader calls that see only the document then answer the questions each reader needs to act on, and code counts the answers.
exam_tip: Look for the option that shows alternatives, measured trade-offs and a reversal condition, tailored per audience. Answers that hide alternatives, send everyone the same summary, or pass raw technical detail to executives are distractors.
headline: Show what you traded away, in their units.

concepts.b: Measure each option on the client's own eval data. The accountable stakeholder owns the choice, so they must see the alternatives, not only the pick.
The COO thinks in money, staff time and service; IT security in data, access and controls. Same facts, different order and units.

concepts.t: A decision record outlives the meeting
concepts.b: Context, options, decision, consequences and status, written down. A newcomer can then see why, instead of accepting or reversing it blindly.
A measured result that would change the decision, such as weekly accuracy below 90% for two weeks. It turns a debate into a monitor.
A model swap behind a stable interface is cheap to undo. Data-residency or write-access decisions are not, and get the full analysis and sign-off.

task_title: Manage stakeholder feedback loops and expectation alignment (including SLAs)
title: "99.99% and always correct" breaks on day one: commit to measured SLOs
stem: Lumen's COO wants the board pack to promise that the store assistant will be available 99.99% of the time and that its answers will always be correct. The six-week pilot in 20 stores measured 99.82% availability, a p95 latency of 2.4 seconds and 374 correct answers out of 400 graded by product specialists. What should you propose?

options.A: Accept 99.99% availability and always-correct answers as stretch goals in the board pack, and report progress against both of those targets every month.
options.B: Commit to 99.99% availability by moving to a multi-region deployment, and replace the accuracy promise with a disclaimer that answers may sometimes be wrong.
options.C: Make no service commitment in the board pack until the assistant has run in production for six months and there is more data to go on.
options.D: Agree SLOs from the pilot results for availability, latency, accuracy on a graded sample and hand-over time, with an error budget and a monthly review.

why: Commitments a stakeholder can rely on come from measurement. Operational targets (availability, latency, hand-over time) are set where the pilot already meets them; accuracy is a rate on a stated graded sample, because 374 of 400 is an estimate, not a per-answer guarantee. An error budget says what happens when the misses add up, and a regular review with store operations keeps expectations and feedback aligned.

wrong.A: A target the pilot already misses is broken on the day it is promised, and "always correct" is not a property any model-based system can measure or keep.
wrong.B: More regions may lift availability, but it is engineering to a wish at unknown cost, and a disclaimer removes the quality commitment instead of measuring it.
wrong.C: Six months without agreed targets leaves the board with no expectations and the team with no feedback loop, so the misalignment simply grows.

fix: Set SLOs from measured pilot results, state quality as a sampled rate, attach an error budget and run a regular feedback review.
see: Phase 1's commitments are already breached by the pilot; Phase 2's are all met, with an error budget and a review cadence.
explain: Both phases answer the sponsor's same request. Phase 1 writes her wish into the board pack, and code finds the pilot already misses it: 99.82% availability against 99.99%, 93.5% accuracy against near-perfect. Phase 2 reads the pilot first with get_pilot_metrics, sets each target the pilot meets, measures accuracy and critical errors on a graded sample with its size stated, adds an error budget that freezes changes when spent, and names an owner and a review cadence. The sponsor's original ask goes back to her with the evidence.
exam_tip: For LLM systems, accept answers that split operational SLOs from quality measured on a sample, and that pair targets with an error budget and a review cadence. Reject "always correct", stretch targets the evidence already misses, and deferring commitments altogether.
headline: Promise what you measured. Budget the misses.

concepts.b: An SLI is a measure (p95 latency). An SLO is a target for it (3 s or less). An SLA is the agreement with consequences when an SLO is missed.
Operational SLOs are measured on every request. Quality SLOs, such as accuracy, are rates estimated on a graded sample, so the sample size is part of the promise.
374 correct out of 400 is 93.5%, but the Wilson 95% interval runs from about 90.6% to 95.5%. Promise below the lower bound, not at the point estimate.

concepts.t: Error budgets turn arguments into rules
concepts.b: 99.5% availability allows about 126 minutes of store hours a month. When it is spent, changes stop until reliability is fixed.

concepts.t: Feedback has a cadence and an owner
concepts.b: A monthly review of the SLOs, store feedback and the weekly graded sample, chaired by a named owner, keeps expectations and the system aligned.

task_title: Document architectures and provide implementation guidance
title: A summary drops the runbook and owners: hand off an ADR and a guide
stem: Your engagement with Lumen Retail ends in three weeks. Lumen's in-house team will then run the product-support assistant and change its prompts, retrieval and model on their own. Which documentation best prepares them to do that without you?

options.A: An ADR per key decision with its context, consequences and rejected alternatives, plus an implementation guide with interfaces, the pinned model ID, runbooks and owners.
options.B: The final steering-committee slide deck with the architecture diagram, the business case and the pilot results, saved on the shared drive where the team can find it later.
options.C: Recorded walkthrough sessions in which the architect explains the code, prompts and retrieval set-up, so the team can replay them whenever a question comes up after handoff.
options.D: Thorough comments throughout the code, prompts and configuration files, so the documentation lives next to the implementation and stays in step with every future change.

why: A receiving team needs the why, the how and the who. Architecture Decision Records keep the context, the consequences and the alternatives that lost, so a later change is made knowingly. The implementation guide keeps the exact interfaces, the pinned model ID and where it is set, numbered runbook steps with thresholds, and a named owner for each part.

wrong.B: A steering deck is written for executives: it carries the business case, not the interfaces, runbook steps or owners an engineer needs at 2 a.m.
wrong.C: Recordings cannot be searched or versioned, and they still leave decisions, thresholds and owners for the team to dig out of hours of video.
wrong.D: Code comments explain local behaviour; they cannot hold why alternatives were rejected, the runbook, or who owns the prompt and the eval suite.

fix: Hand off an ADR per decision and an implementation guide with interfaces, configuration, runbooks and named owners.
see: The summary has none of the nine sections and the newcomer can answer few questions; ADR-007 and the guide have all nine and the newcomer answers all five.
explain: Both phases document the same working notes. Phase 1 writes the usual high-level summary: accurate, readable, and missing what the team needs once the architect has gone. Phase 2 writes ADR-007 (context, decision, status, consequences, alternatives considered) and an implementation guide (interfaces, configuration, runbook, owners). Code checks the nine sections by heading. A new Lumen developer, a separate Claude call that sees only the document, then answers five handoff questions, and code checks each answer for the key fact: claude-haiku-5-5, the /assist fields, the catalogue index check, Arun Pillai, and Sonnet 5.5 as the rejected option.
exam_tip: When the question is about handoff to another team, pick the answer that records decisions with their alternatives and gives actionable implementation detail: interfaces, configuration, runbooks and owners. Decks, recordings and code comments each cover only part of it.
headline: Write down the why, the how and the who.

concepts.b: Title, context, decision, status, consequences, and the alternatives that lost. A superseded ADR is marked, not deleted, so the history stays readable.
In a Claude system the model ID, prompts, tools, retrieval corpus and evals shape behaviour. Each must be versioned and documented, not only the code.

concepts.t: Pin and record the model ID
concepts.b: Name the exact model ID and the file it is set in. A change of model is a release, gated by the eval suite like any prompt change.
"Escalation rate above 12% for two days: check index freshness, re-run evals, roll back if below 92%" can be acted on. "Monitor quality" cannot.
Prompt and evals, retrieval index, on-call, and the decision itself. Without owners, a handoff becomes a question nobody can answer.

task_title: Support lifecycle phases (discovery, design, handoff, monitoring, iteration)
title: Drift found 3 weeks late by a complaint: monitors that re-run evals
stem: Lumen's store assistant goes live on 1 March, and Lumen's in-house team takes it over six weeks later. Lumen launches a new product range every season, and the pilot's escalation rate was 8%. Which plan best supports the solution after go-live?

options.A: Close the project once the go-live acceptance tests pass, and have the support desk raise tickets whenever store staff report wrong or unhelpful answers to them.
options.B: Freeze the prompt, model and catalogue index at go-live so the validated behaviour cannot drift, and re-certify the whole system once a year.
options.C: Set monitors with thresholds and owners, such as escalation-rate drift or a new range, that send changes back through evaluation, and hand off against criteria.
options.D: Keep the architect on a retainer to review the dashboards every month and decide, case by case, when the assistant needs to be changed, retuned or retrained.

why: After go-live the inputs keep changing: a new range brings new products and harder questions, and the model itself will eventually be retired. A lifecycle plan names the signals that matter, sets thresholds from the pilot baseline, gives each an owner, and routes every triggered change back through the eval suite before it ships. The handoff is passed on criteria the receiving team proves, not on a date.

wrong.A: Waiting for staff complaints finds drift weeks late, and closing at go-live leaves nobody owning the system's behaviour once the architect has gone.
wrong.B: Freezing the system does not freeze its inputs: a new range still arrives, and the frozen index and prompt fall further behind every season.
wrong.D: A monthly review by one person has no defined triggers, cannot catch a drift between reviews, and keeps the receiving team dependent instead of handing off.

fix: Plan monitoring signals with thresholds, owners and an action that re-runs the evals, and hand off against criteria with evidence.
see: Phase 1 finds the drift in week 8 from a complaint; Phase 2's monitors send the change back to the eval suite in week 5 or 6.
explain: Both phases plan the same assistant from the same facts. Phase 1's project template ends at go-live and closes, so when the spring range lands in week 5 and escalations climb from 8% to 15%, the first signal is store managers complaining to the COO in week 8. Phase 2's lifecycle template adds monitoring and iteration: monitors with thresholds from the pilot baseline (escalation rate, weekly graded accuracy, a catalogue-change event), an owner each, and the action rerun_eval_suite_and_iterate. Code replays the same ten weeks against both plans and reports the week each drift is acted on, and Phase 2 also lists handoff criteria with their evidence.
exam_tip: Pick the answer that keeps the system in a loop after launch: defined signals and thresholds, named owners, changes that return to evaluation, and a handoff with exit criteria. Closing at go-live, freezing the system or relying on one person's review are the distractors.
headline: Go-live is a phase. Monitors start the next loop.

concepts.b: Discovery, design, build, pilot, go-live, handoff, monitoring, iteration. Iteration returns to design or evaluation; the system is never finished.
Input drift (new products, new questions), business change, and the model lifecycle: every model ID is eventually deprecated and retired.
The pilot measured an 8% escalation rate. A monitor at 11% for a week acts long before 15%; one at 16% never fires.

concepts.t: Every change goes back through the evals
concepts.b: A new range, a prompt edit or a model swap re-runs the eval suite before release. The suite built in the pilot is what makes iteration cheap.

concepts.t: Handoff on evidence, not a date
concepts.b: The receiving team proves it can run the system: a change shipped on its own with an eval report, and a rehearsed runbook.

task_title: Configure Claude tools and environments for teams (e.g., Claude Code)
title: The team's rules live on one laptop: commit the Claude Code config
stem: Kestrel is rolling Claude Code out to 40 engineers in four squads. Today each engineer keeps the team's conventions and permissions in their own ~/.claude files; two of them allow Bash(*), and one has a Sentry token pasted into a personal MCP config. A new engineer's first sessions follow none of the conventions. What should the platform team do?

options.A: Publish the recommended ~/.claude settings on the team wiki, and ask each engineer to copy them onto their own machine as part of their onboarding.
options.B: Commit a project CLAUDE.md, .claude/settings.json allow and deny rules, shared skills and an .mcp.json that reads its token from an environment variable.
options.C: Put the team's conventions, permission rules and each MCP server's token into one shared CLAUDE.md at the repository root, so that every session reads them.
options.D: Have each squad lead review their engineers' ~/.claude folders every quarter, and remove any risky permissions or pasted tokens that they find in them.

why: Configuration in the repository reaches every engineer's session from the first run and changes only through review. CLAUDE.md carries the guidance Claude reads; .claude/settings.json carries allow and deny rules the harness enforces; shared skills give everyone the same workflows; and .mcp.json can reference ${SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN}, so the secret stays in each engineer's environment and out of git.

wrong.A: Copied personal settings drift from day one, nobody can see what each engineer actually runs, and the team still has no shared deny rules.
wrong.C: CLAUDE.md is guidance Claude reads, not permissions the harness enforces, and tokens written into a committed file are secrets in git.
wrong.D: A quarterly review watches the risk instead of removing it: between reviews Bash(*) and pasted tokens stay live, and new engineers still get nothing.

fix: Commit CLAUDE.md, .claude/settings.json allow/deny rules, shared skills and an .mcp.json that uses environment variables for secrets.
see: Phase 1: Ben's session loads 0 of 5 team policies. Phase 2: all 5 reach his first session, and Claude's report of what loads matches the loader.
explain: Both phases ask what a new engineer's first session loads in kestrel/checkout-service. In Phase 1 the conventions live in Ana's ~/.claude files, so Ben's session, which sees only the repository, loads no instruction file, no deny rule, no skill and no MCP server; Ana's own config meanwhile allows Bash(*) and holds a literal token that no review sees. In Phase 2 the same conventions are committed, with the token replaced by ${SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN}. Claude inspects the files with Glob and Read and reports what loads; plain code computes the same and checks five team policies.
exam_tip: For team-wide Claude Code behaviour, choose committed project configuration: CLAUDE.md for guidance, .claude/settings.json for enforced permissions, .claude/skills/ for shared workflows, and .mcp.json with environment-variable references. Organisation-wide must-holds go further, into managed settings.
headline: Put each rule where every session loads it.

concepts.b: ~/.claude reaches only you. .claude/settings.json and CLAUDE.md in the repository reach everyone. .claude/settings.local.json is yours, kept out of git.
CLAUDE.md and skills are read by Claude and followed most of the time. Permission rules, hooks and managed settings are enforced by the harness.
Permission lists combine across scopes, and a deny anywhere beats an allow. A team deny on git push --force holds even if someone allows more.
A skill in .claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md gives all 40 engineers the same /pr-review workflow, versioned and reviewed like code.
Commit .mcp.json with ${SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN}; each engineer's environment supplies the value. A token written into the file is a secret in git.

task_title: Improve developer workflows using AI-assisted tooling
title: A chat review can't block PR 512: run claude -p in CI behind a gate
stem: Kestrel engineers paste diffs into a Claude chat for review when they remember to, each with their own prompt, and the feedback varies from person to person. Last month a refund change that logged full card numbers was merged. The platform team wants consistent reviews that stop changes like that. What should they do?

options.A: Add a CONTRIBUTING.md rule that every engineer must ask Claude to review the diff in a chat before opening a pull request.
options.B: Give each engineer a recommended review prompt to keep in their personal ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, so every review starts from the same text.
options.C: Have Claude review each pull request in CI and post its findings as a free-text comment for the human reviewer to read before merging.
options.D: Run claude -p in CI with a committed review skill and a JSON schema for findings, and fail the check on any high-severity finding.

why: The improvement comes from wiring the tool into the flow, not from using it more often. CI runs the review on every pull request; the committed skill applies the same rules for everyone; the schema makes the output something a script can read; and a few lines of plain code fail the check on a high-severity finding, so branch protection stops the merge. The model supplies the judgement, the gate is deterministic.

wrong.A: A written rule still depends on each engineer remembering and on their own prompt, and its prose output cannot block anything.
wrong.B: A personal ~/.claude file reaches only its owner, drifts over time, and still produces nothing a pipeline can check.
wrong.C: Running in CI fixes when it happens, but free text cannot gate a merge: a busy reviewer can still miss the finding.

fix: Run the team's review skill with claude -p in CI, emit findings against a schema, and let a plain-code gate fail the check on high severity.
see: Phase 1's chat reply is prose and the gate has no verdict; Phase 2 blocks PR 512 on KR-1 at refund.py line 14 and passes the clean PR 513.
explain: Both phases review the same pull request, which logs card.number on line 14 and sends no Idempotency-Key. Phase 1 is the ad hoc chat: helpful prose, often even naming the problem, but nothing the pipeline can act on. Phase 2 runs claude -p in CI with the committed pr-review skill (rules KR-1 to KR-4) and a findings schema on PR 512 and on a clean PR 513. A gate in plain code parses the findings and exits 1 on any high-severity finding: PR 512 is blocked, PR 513 passes.
exam_tip: When the goal is consistent, enforced AI assistance across a team, look for the answer that runs in the shared pipeline, uses committed configuration, and produces structured output a deterministic step can gate on. Free-text comments and personal prompts are partial fixes.
headline: Wire it into the flow. Gate on structure.

concepts.b: Print mode runs one prompt and exits, which suits CI. --output-format json gives a result a script can read instead of a chat transcript.
A committed .claude/skills/pr-review/SKILL.md gives every run the same rules, versioned and reviewed like code.
A JSON schema for findings (file, line, rule, severity) lets a CI step count and filter them. Prose needs a human to read it.

concepts.t: Model for judgement, code for the gate
concepts.b: Claude decides whether line 14 logs a card number. Plain code decides that a high finding fails the build. Branch protection blocks the merge.
Faster code writing helps only if review and verification keep up. Automating the first review pass keeps the human reviewer for judgement.

task_title: Support debugging and operational issue resolution
title: 6% of summaries fail: trace stop_reason max_tokens, don't guess
stem: Since Tuesday afternoon, 6% of requests to Kestrel's order-summary service, which uses Claude to write the summary on the order confirmation page, fail with "Order summary unavailable". The on-call engineer asks Claude Code for help. Which approach best resolves the incident?

options.A: Give Claude read-only access to logs, traces and recent deploys, and have it reproduce a failing request, test one hypothesis at a time and verify the fix before rollout.
options.B: Paste the alert and the customer ticket into Claude, apply the most likely fix it suggests straight away, and roll it back if the error rate has not dropped within an hour.
options.C: Switch the service to a larger Claude model, because failures that start without any application code change usually point to a regression in the quality of the model's output.
options.D: Wrap the Claude call in a retry with exponential backoff, so that transient failures are absorbed and customers stop seeing errors while the team investigates the cause.

why: Claude is useful in an incident when it works from evidence. Read-only access to logs, traces and deploys is safe to grant widely and lets it see that every failing trace stops with stop_reason max_tokens at 1,024 tokens after a config change halved max_tokens. Reproducing a failing request, testing one hypothesis at a time and verifying the fix in staging turns a plausible story into a proven cause before anything changes in production.

wrong.B: A fix chosen from symptoms is a guess; applying it in production risks a second incident and teaches nothing if the errors happen to stop.
wrong.C: The failures began with a config change, not a model change; a larger model costs more and still stops at the same max_tokens limit.
wrong.D: A truncated response is deterministic for that order: every retry hits the same max_tokens limit, so retries add latency and cost without fixing it.

fix: Read logs, traces and deploys; reproduce a failing request; change one setting at a time; verify the fix before rollout.
see: Phase 1 cannot name a proven cause; Phase 2 finds stop_reason max_tokens after config v42, reproduces it and verifies the fix in staging.
explain: Both phases start from the same page and ticket. With symptoms only, Claude can offer a story or a to-do list, and nothing stands behind it. With read-only search_logs, list_traces, get_trace and list_deploys, plus rerun_request in staging, Claude finds a new JSONDecodeError group from Tue 14:05, failing traces on large orders that all stop with stop_reason max_tokens at 1,024 output tokens, and config v42 halving max_tokens. It reproduces the failure, verifies that a higher limit returns end_turn with valid JSON, and rules out the get_inventory timeout, which runs at the same rate as before.
exam_tip: In debugging questions, prefer evidence-driven loops: observability access, reproduction, one change at a time, verification before rollout. Retries, model upgrades and fixes guessed from symptoms are distractors, especially when the failure is deterministic, such as a max_tokens truncation.
headline: Read the trace before you trust the theory.

concepts.t: stop_reason tells you why it stopped
concepts.b: end_turn means Claude finished. max_tokens means the reply was cut off at the limit; parsing that text as JSON then fails with a confusing error.
Record model, max_tokens, input and output tokens, stop_reason, latency and tool calls per request. Most Claude incidents show up in these fields.
Read-only access to logs, traces and deploys is safe to grant for diagnosis. Changes go through a branch, review and an approved rollout.
Replay a failing request as it was sent. If it fails the same way, change one setting and re-run: a pass is evidence, not a hope.
A transient 529 is worth a retry. A reply truncated by max_tokens fails the same way every time, so a retry only adds latency and cost.
